summary: Replication package for the article "Example Scenarios, Random Sequences or Contract-Guided Exploration? Testing a Stateful Learning Agreement Service with Language Model Implementations, Seeded Faults and Blind Test Suites" (I. Tiievskyi). The study compares three black-box testing techniques on an executable contract of a learning agreement revision service inspired by the Erasmus Without Paper (EWP) Outgoing Mobility Learning Agreements workflow: example scenarios (EX), random request sequences (RND) and contract-guided breadth-first exploration (SYS). The package contains everything needed to rerun the experiments and recompute the reported numbers. Contents - contract/: the executable contract (ten obligations), a description of which parts of the EWP workflow it covers, the reference implementation REF with ten dependent faults, the fourteen example scenarios (EX) and unit tests. - study/impl_I1, study/impl_I2, study/i3: five implementations in total – REF plus I1 (Python) and I2 (Node.js) written from the contract and interface only, and I3 and I4 written by two further language models from the same brief; implementers' notes on ambiguities and file hashes. - study/faults, study/mutants_ext: 40 seeded mutants (F01–F10, G01–G10, GM01–GM10, PM01–PM10) with their catalogue, exact edits, revealing sequences and seeding briefs. - study/human_faults: ten faults (H01–H10) written by a backend developer without AI tools, together with the task sheet stating the inclusion criteria. - study/blind: ten example suites written by six language models from the contract text alone, the writers' brief, the pre-registered evaluation harness with its hashes, the corrected harness and the results before and after the correction. - study/harness, study/controls, study/robustness: the test bench (EX, RND, SYS, differential oracle), the black-box contract observer, oracle and budget controls, the census of disagreements between implementations, observation-level, pruning, hash-seed and fault-mechanism analyses, and regression tests of the scenario comparator. - Raw results (JSON) for every reported table; README.md maps each table of the article to the script and result file that produce it. Requirements and use Python 3.11 or later and Node.js 18 or later, standard libraries only, no network access. Each script is run from its own folder; a run of 20,000 requests takes about 5 seconds. README.md gives quick checks, the exact commands for the full blind-suite run and the census reproduction, and the random seeds used (RND seeds 1–5, 1–10 for the dependent faults, census seed 1, PYTHONHASHSEED 0 for the robustness analyses). Version 1.1 The census of disagreements now draws the request selected from history from a local generator initialised with the census seed, so the census is fully reproducible. All ten pairwise census runs were repeated; the sets of disagreements and the first detection of each point reported in Table 5 are unchanged. The version 1.0 census results are kept in study/census_v1.0. The main mutant and blind-suite runs are not affected by this change. Provenance The contract, the reference implementation, the example scenarios, the dependent faults, the harness and the analysis scripts were prepared by the author with AI assistance (Claude Opus 5.5). I1, I2 and F01–G10 were written by isolated Claude Opus 5.5 agents without access to the tests; I3, I4, GM01–GM10 and PM01–PM10 by GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon from the same briefs; the blind suites by Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.2, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon. The archived briefs cover the blind suites, I3/I4, the GM/PM mutants and the developer task; full agent and chat transcripts are not included. The developer agreed to the publication of the faults. Integrity SHA256SUMS lists the SHA-256 checksum of every file in the package (sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS in the package root).
title: Replication package: Example Scenarios, Random Sequences or Contract-Guided Exploration? Testing a Stateful Learning Agreement Service

summary: Contents This release provides the NN-FF-FD-RA numerical implementation, training and evaluation scripts, selected trained model artifacts, archived evaluation arrays, and reproducibility materials. Included materials comprise: Training dataset and baseline, V3, and original pointwise RA model checkpoints, normalization parameters, and training summaries. Archived evaluation artifacts for TEST28, TEST29, TEST37, and TEST38S. Error-distribution metrics used by the result-export workflow. REPRODUCIBILITY_MANIFEST.csv , including file sizes and SHA-256 checksums. The original pointwise RA lineage is preserved. The separate grouped-split RA candidate is not substituted in this release. Reproducibility scope The archived evaluation arrays provide the inputs used by the result-export script to regenerate the corresponding manuscript tables, figures, and summary. The release also provides selected training data, checkpoints, normalization parameters, and workflows for inspection and use. It does not claim that every experiment or every reported result can be reproduced end-to-end from the released files alone. See README.md for execution instructions and reproducibility limitations. summary: POLYPHENOL-LIPID COUPLING SCIENCE F096-F100 | Family 20 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch  |  33 x STARLI  |  Edition v1.0 / November 2026 A companion to the 819-page integrated research atlas: molecular interface binding, oil-peroxide kinetics, polyphenol redox depletion, genuine lipid nanocarrier co-loading, and nonclinical barrier/viability evidence. Editorial scope and safety boundary This is a prospective research design, not a report of completed experiments. The graphical response surfaces are synthetic and reproducible. Traditional materia-medica scholarship is used as a source of research questions, not as a substitute for evidence of human tolerance or cosmetic efficacy. Source-lineage and the native endpoints are inherited from the 817-page STARLI Master Blueprint F096-F100; the narrative and candidate models are newly elaborated research proposals. A five-part chain of polyphenol-lipid-botanical causation F096 - Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Interfacial Binding at the Limit: primary endpoint apparent binding constant K_app (L/mol). Fair comparator: free polyphenol alone, free oil/lipid alone, missing-component mixtures and matched blank liposomes. Disqualifying counterexample: surface adsorption, self-quenching, polyphenol autoxidation, incomplete recovery or bilayer disruption masquerading as molecular binding. F097 - Botanical Polyphenol-Plant Oil Antioxidant Coupling at the Limit: primary endpoint plant-oil peroxide formation rate (meq peroxide/kg oil per h). Fair comparator: polyphenol-free oil, oil-free polyphenol, matched vehicle, dark isothermal control and tocopherol reference. Disqualifying counterexample: autooxidation, probe quenching, transient induction-period selection or peroxide breakdown without suppressed secondary oxidation. F098 - Lipid Oxidation and Botanical Polyphenol Activity at the Limit: primary endpoint slope of polyphenol depletion versus lipid oxidation (prespecified native units). Fair comparator: unprotected oil, polyphenol without oil, oxidized-polyphenol spike and matched light-oxygen factorial controls. Disqualifying counterexample: reverse causality, time-confounded oxidation, ion suppression or antioxidant depletion without protection of the lipid phase. F099 - Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Nano-Codelivery at the Limit: primary endpoint true co-loading fraction (%) of independently qualified polyphenol and lipid compartments. Fair comparator: free botanical in oil, empty carriers, equal-total-mass physically blended carriers and independent single-loaded formulations. Disqualifying counterexample: adsorption to particle surface, unseparated micelles, centrifugation loss or fluorescent overlap mistaken for shared nanocarrier loading. F100 - Barrier Evidence for Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Formulations at the Limit: primary endpoint joint qualified barrier-surrogate effect and RhE viability (%), reported separately. Fair comparator: vehicle-matched control, polyphenol-only, lipid-only, blank carrier and positive reference irritant. Disqualifying counterexample: optical-probe self-quenching, surface occlusion, damaged RhE tissue, dye interference or unmatched vehicle causing false barrier evidence. Methodological introduction F096: apparent interfacial association is not proof of binding Different redox states and lipids require independent molecular identity. A change in fluorescence or oil-water partition can arise from self-quenching, adsorption or photochemical loss. An apparent binding constant must survive reversible washout, recovery checks and a separately measured lipid interface area. F098: oxidative depletion and lipid preservation are different A statistical slope between polyphenol depletion and lipid oxidation is a descriptive estimate, not a causal mechanism. Independently perturb oxygen and photon exposure, quantify oxidized parent molecules, and identify whether high-dose polyphenols can switch from inhibitory to pro-oxid

summary: HighSchoolBench is a multimodal benchmark designed to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on authentic high-school assessment questions. It contains 10,501 question–answer pairs drawn from standardized assessments, U.S. state examinations, and academic competitions across 11 subjects. The dataset was constructed using optical character recognition (OCR), source-specific preprocessing, LLM-based structured extraction, and validation against original assessment materials and answer keys. Dataset components The benchmark consists of two components: HighSchoolBench-MCQ: Contains 7,549 multiple-choice questions, including single-answer and multiple-answer questions. Answer options may be represented as text, images, or tables. The dataset is organized into 15 configurations based on the modalities of the question context and answer options. HighSchoolBench-OEQ: Contains 2,952 open-ended questions with free-text reference answers. These include worked solutions, explanations and descriptions, multi-part responses, and exact or short scientific answers. The dataset is organized into 18 configurations based on the supporting context and expected answer form. Questions may include supporting text, images, tables, or combinations of these modalities. Dataset structure The HighSchoolBench archive is organized into two components: multiple-choice questions (MCQ) and open-ended questions (OEQ). Both components are grouped by question configuration and dataset split. (18 configurations in total) │ └── README.md Each configuration directory contains the available train , validation , and/or test splits. metadata.jsonl contains the questions, reference answers, and associated metadata. images/ contains the image files referenced by the corresponding JSONL records, where applicable. README.md provides dataset documentation, configuration descriptions, and usage instructions. The MCQ and OEQ components can be accessed independently. For benchmarking, researchers can select the relevant configurations based on the modalities supported by their models. summary: In the Standard Model of particle physics, the Cabibbo--Kobayashi--Maskawa (CKM) quark mixing matrix requires four unconstrained empirical parameters: three inter-generational mixing angles ($\theta_{12}^{\text{CKM}}, \theta_{23}^{\text{CKM}}, \theta_{13}^{\text{CKM}}$, or $|V_{us}|, |V_{cb}|, |V_{ub}|$) and one CP-violating phase ($\delta_{\text{CP}}^{\text{CKM}}$). summary: This record contains model-ready data supporting the manuscript "Reference-Aware Evaluation of Neural Surrogates for Shallow-Water Flows: A Controlled Multi-Reference Computational-Fluid Benchmark". The manuscript is currently in submission. The main dataset covers 13,500 shared synthetic scenarios: 10,000 for training, 1,000 for validation, and 2,500 for testing. The common-time outputs use the same 50 requested evaluation times for all three references, from 8.4 to 420 benchmark-time units. Each solver keeps its own natural time steps; interpolation is used only to form outputs at the requested times. The references are the Hydrostatic and MUSCL-HR shallow-water solvers and a study-defined elevation-only, linear, weakly dispersive Boussinesq-type reference. The record includes the main processed datasets for each reference; additional processed data on 32×32, 64×64, and 128×128 grids; pooled-reference data for models trained without solver identity and models given the requested reference as an input; and an auxiliary archive of evaluation settings and preprocessing configurations for the train, validation, and test splits. The release manifest lists the archive contents. Each large archive is split into numbered, byte-exact parts of up to 1.8 GB. Download every part for an archive, concatenate the parts in numeric order, and use the supplied SHA-256 files to verify both the parts and the reconstructed archive. See README.md for commands. These data are synthetic and cover a finite benchmark horizon. They do not establish performance for real events, site-specific hazard forecasting, or operational tsunami warning. Spatial coordinates and time values use the benchmark's own scales; they are not calibrated to real locations or physical time. Source code and experiment documentation are available in the project repository . The raw numerical-reference data are described in the companion raw-data record.
title: Tsunami-Surrogate Common-Time Benchmark: Model-Ready Multi-Reference Data

summary: Version 1.1.0 of the reproducible research repository accompanying the manuscript: "Operative treatment of pyogenic spondylodiscitis in German hospitals: patient selection, hospital size, and in-hospital mortality" This release adds a cell-level reconstruction of the hospital tables (bed-size class × ownership). The InEK DatenBrowser combines some cells of these tables into a residual row, differently in each query and not only for small counts, so the displayed cells give numerators and denominators that do not match. The reconstruction (analysis/05b_hospital_reconstruction.py) resolves the hidden cells under the containment constraints between the four queries of each year; reported values are medians over 2000 feasible reconstructions, with ranges over these and 2000 extreme reconstructions (fixed seed). With the reconstruction, the operative share is 28.2% in hospitals with fewer than 300 beds and 63.7% in hospitals with 1000 beds or more (version 1.0.0: 27.9% and 65.2%). The risk ratio stratified by data year and hospital bed-size category is 1.02 (95% CI 0.96–1.08), and by data year and ownership 1.08 (1.01–1.14). Also added: hospital-stratified risk ratios, article tables, figure data and key numbers (analysis/06_reported_quantities.py) and the article figures (analysis/07_article_figures.py). All other results are unchanged. Intraspinal abscess (G06.1) is now labelled intraspinal empyema. The underlying hospital data are publicly accessible through the InEK DatenBrowser. Original query outputs are not redistributed; they can be regenerated from the documented query specification.
title: Operative treatment and in-hospital mortality in pyogenic spondylodiscitis: query protocol, analysis code and derived results

summary: Markov chains for a Bayesian inverse problem with a 100-parameter Karhunen-Loeve log permeability field and an elliptic PDE, following P. G. Constantine, C. Kent and T. Bui-Thanh, "Accelerating Markov chain Monte Carlo with active subspaces", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 38(5):A2779-A2805, 2016, doi:10.1137/15M1042127. pde_mcmc_chains.npz (load with numpy.load, no pickle) holds the synthetic data, the misfit gradients at 1000 prior samples and their active subspace, 20 random-walk Metropolis chains and 4 + 4 active-variable chains (reductions), and a grid of the misfit on the active variables. kl-short.npz is the Karhunen-Loeve basis the model uses. generate_data.py in the repository regenerates the chains from saved seeds. These files are deposited as the full-size archive of the data set uq_benchmarks/PDE_Inverse_Problem_MCMC in the as-data-sets repository ( https://github.com/paulcon/as-data-sets/tree/main/uq_benchmarks/PDE_Inverse_Problem_MCMC ), a collection of Jupyter notebooks that apply active subspaces (parameter-space dimension reduction) to science and engineering models. The notebook there analyzes these data; its DATA.md documents every file, column, unit and unknown. The repository keeps each file under 10 MB, so it ships the same arrays split into files under 10 MB. License: CC BY 4.0. Cite Constantine, Kent and Bui-Thanh (2016).
title: Markov chain Monte Carlo on the active variables of a PDE inverse problem: chains, subspace and grid

summary: BOTANICAL SHEET-MASK SCIENCE: FROM SERUM CHEMISTRY TO VERIFIED WET CONTACT F121-F125 | Family 25 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch | 33 x STARLI | Edition v1.0 / November 2026 Five integrated nonclinical research themes: storage marker integrity, lyocell sorption, three-dimensional wet contact, mass-based evaporation and qualified reconstructed-epidermis evidence. Scope and scientific authority This long-form technical notebook is a proposed investigation, not a laboratory or cosmetic product performance report. The primary source is the 817-page STARLI Botanical Master Blueprint v1.0, Family25 F121-F125; older Mothers F12 and F28 provide method and evidence constraints. The numerical charts are synthetic hypotheses. Chinese materia medica inspires provenance, processing and compound questions, not a biological proof. Claims about a commercial sheet mask, sensitive-skin suitability and humans would need independent ethically and legally appropriate evidence. Five different objects, five different vetoes F121 - Botanical Sheet-Mask Serum Active Stability at the Limit. Native measurement: stored mask-serum marker retention (%). Fair reference: equal-formula serum stored in an inert vessel, blank lyocell, matched nonwoven mask and light/dark paired packaging. Disqualifying rival: adsorption onto cellulose, packaging migration, altered extract recovery, optical co-elution or oxygen-driven degradation. F122 - Lyocell–Botanical Serum Adsorption at the Limit. Native measurement: identified botanical marker adsorbed on lyocell (mg/g). Fair reference: matched nonwoven material, no-sheet serum reservoir, same-area inert substrate and prewetted lyocell control. Disqualifying rival: surface liquid mistaken for bonded sorbate, unequal sheet density, incomplete desorption or retained marker counted as delivered. F123 - Botanical Mask Conformability and Liquid Distribution at the Limit. Native measurement: verified face-surface wet-contact area (cm2). Fair reference: shape-matched nonwoven mask, same-serum container exposure, equal-load flat phantom and reversed sheet orientation. Disqualifying rival: pressure shadows mistaken for contact, pixel threshold bias, droplet pooling in folds or high contact area with low local transfer. F124 - Botanical Mask Wear Time and Evaporation at the Limit. Native measurement: evaporation mass flux (g/m2/h). Fair reference: no-sheet serum film, humidity-matched nonwoven, impermeable occlusive reference and evaporation-free gravimetric blank. Disqualifying rival: short-term occlusion masquerades as barrier repair, variable wet area, edge leakage or ambient humidity drift. F125 - Botanical Nano-Sheet-Mask Sensitive-Skin Tolerability at the Limit. Native measurement: qualified reconstructed epidermis viability (%) and marker exposure (microg/cm2). Fair reference: same-contact-time matched serum alone, blank lyocell, nonwoven sheet with matched vehicle and qualified positive-irritant reference. Disqualifying rival: pigmented botanicals distort viability reagent, local occlusion hides evaporation, tissue necrosis mimics reduced flux or uncontrolled dose. Methodological sources and foundations Five independent scientific identities under one mask F121 tests marker retention through storage without confusing cellulose sorption with degradation. F122 resolves lyocell-bound and freely available serum markers. F123 measures the genuine 3D wet-contact area and spatial transfer rather than a photographic silhouette. F124 reconstructs evaporation by mass, time, true area and environmental gradients. F125 tests qualified RhE viability only with chemically verified exposure, matched vehicle and cell-free interference controls. None of the five outputs substitutes for another. F121: chemical stability versus package partition A marker lost from the liquid phase may reside inside lyocell, on packaging film, in a precipitate or as a true degradation product. The difference is decisive. I

summary: In the loop-erased ant process of Kious, Mailler and Schapira, ants walk in turn from a nest $N$ to a food source $F$ on a finite graph, and each ant reinforces the loop-erasure of its time-reversed trajectory. Kious, Mailler and Schapira conjectured that the weight of an edge grows linearly exactly when the edge lies on a geodesic from $N$ to $F$. Let $G_\ell$ consist of a triangle $N,u,v$ and two paths of $\ell$ edges, from $u$ to $F$ and from $v$ to $F$. On $G_\ell$ the normalised weights converge almost surely, and the limit on the edge $uv$ is $(1-1/\ell)\rho(1-\rho)$ for a non-degenerate random variable $\rho$ with values in $(0,1)$. For $\ell\ge2$ this edge lies on no geodesic, so the conjecture fails; for $\ell=1$, the losange, the edge dies. The same statements hold for the forward-loop-erased process of Armfield and Mailler, which has the same law.
title: A non-geodesic edge that survives in the loop-erased ant process

summary: Companion deposit for the conference paper "One Coefficient Is Not Enough: A Pre-specified Replication of the Impostor-Practice Effect on the CMU Keystroke Benchmark" (accepted at AICSET 2026). Killourhy and Maxion (RAID 2010) summarised impostor practice on the CMU benchmark as a single additive coefficient of +1.1 percentage points of equal-error rate in the no-update regime. This deposit re-runs their factorial design without updating — three detectors (scaled Manhattan, outlier count, Mahalanobis nearest neighbour), four training amounts, three feature sets, 51 subjects — and evaluates each of the 36 cells on 16 impostor windows spanning the eight sessions: 576 evaluations. It contains the analysis script, the result file from which every number in the paper is taken, three earlier independent reproductions that the script must match within 1e-12 before reading any cell, the pre-specified protocol (in French, validated on 13 October 2026 before measurement; dated but not lodged in a public registry), and the figure script. The computation is deterministic; a re-run reproduces the result file byte for byte. The CMU benchmark itself is NOT redistributed here. MANIFEST.tsv lists every file with its size and SHA-256; verify_manifest.py recomputes them. See README.md for the two documented differences from the internal working copies (identifiers in the protocol and the protocol file name recorded by the script; no numerical value differs). Version 1.1 adds the post-hoc sensitivity analyses reported in Section 4.6 and Table 3 of the camera-ready paper (src/km_grid_sensitivity.py and results/km_grid_sensitivity.json): a 200 000-resample bootstrap with five seeds, the unpruned-ROC EER, a random practice slope per subject, a paired-difference model, and a comparison with the predictions of Killourhy and Maxion (2010, Table 1). They were decided after peer review and amend no pre-specified reading. No code, result, protocol or figure file of version 1.0 is changed; README.md and MANIFEST.tsv are updated.
title: Impostor practice on the CMU keystroke benchmark: code, results and pre-specified protocol for a replication of Killourhy and Maxion (2010)

summary: This Zenodo archive provides files to train and evaluate machine-learning models for structural annotation of MS/MS spectra. Specifically, we provide Spectraverse, a harmonized and curated resource of publicly available MS/MS spectra. We also provide candidate sets for the molecule retrieval task, in which a model is provided with an MS/MS spectrum and a set of candidate structures and is asked to identify the structure that generated the spectrum in question. Spectraverse The zenodo repo 10.5281/zenodo.23745627 contains following files: File Description spectraverse-1.0.3.mgf MS/MS spectra with their metadata and peak (mz/intensity) information in mgf format spectraverse-1.0.3.csv.gz The metadata for each spectrum in the csv format (without peak information) Spectraverse-1.0.3-candidates-formula.json Formula-based candidate sets: language model-generated structures with the same neutral molecular formula as the ground-truth structure Spectraverse-1.0.3-candidates-mass.json Mass-based candidate sets: language model-generated structures within 10 ppm of the neutral mass of the ground-truth structure Metadata The MGF metadata and the CSV columns contain the following fields. Field Description TITLE Spectrum identifier (for example, SPECTRAVERSE0000000001 ). SMILES , INCHI , INCHIKEY Standardized ground-truth structure. FORMULA , PARENT_MASS Molecular formula and neutral mass of the ground-truth structure PRECURSOR_MZ , ADDUCT , CHARGE , IONMODE Precursor m/z, adduct type, charge, and ionization mode INSTRUMENT_TYPE Instrument type, where reported COLLISION_ENERGY_1 to _3 , NORMALIZED_COLLISION_ENERGY_1 to _3 Up to three collision energies, in eV and NCE.  NUM_PEAKS , MS_LEVEL Number of fragment ions and MS level SOURCE , COMPOUND_NAME Library or publication from which the spectrum was obtained, and compound name FOLD Fold number for cross validation (1 to 10) Candidate sets Each candidate set file contains a single JSON object that maps the SMILES of each ground-truth structure to a list of candidate SMILES: { "<ground-truth SMILES>": ["<ground-truth SMILES>", "<candidate>", "<candidate>", ...], ... } All spectra from the same compound share one candidate set. The ground-truth structure is included in its own candidate set, and is always at the first position. Benchmarking The zenodo repo 10.5281/zenodo.23403402 contains .zip files with scores for each model trained and evaluated in our benchmark. Details of how each model was trained are provided in the Methods section of the corresponding paper (see below). Each .zip file contains one file per candidate set type and test fold, named scores_<formula|mass>_<fold>.txt . Each row in these files corresponds to a single spectrum in their respective test folds and contains values separated by space as: the spectrum TITLE , followed by the score assigned to each candidate structure, in the same order as it appears in the candidate set in the corresponding JSON file. Model evaluation We offer the following guidance for investigators interested in training and evaluating their own models using Spectraverse: Models should be trained exclusively on the ground-truth structures and MS/MS spectra provided in Spectraverse itself, so that differences in model performance can be attributed to modelling decisions rather than the composition of the training dataset or the use of auxiliary data. Investigators who depart from this recommendation, for instance by using pretrained models, synthetic data, or the outputs of auxiliary models (such as predicted molecular formulas), must ensure that the incorporation of such models or data does not result in data leakage, minimally by excluding test spectra and structures from all model components. We refer readers to Liu et al. for a thorough exposition of pitfalls involving data leakage in training machine-learning models for structural annotation of MS/MS spectra For each test fold k , we used fold k − 1 a
title: Comprehensive curation and harmonization of small molecule MS/MS libraries in Spectraverse

summary: GPU-native Julia framework for CT and photon-counting CT simulation, reconstruction, and quantitative spectral imaging. Provides distance-driven forward projection (with Siddon ray tracing as an alternative), polychromatic Beer-Lambert physics with vendor-realistic detector response (MC-derived LUTs for GE Gemstone scintillator and Siemens NAEOTOM Alpha CdTe), FDK, helical WFBP and hybrid iterative reconstruction, sinogram and image-domain beam-hardening correction, projection-domain dual-kVp and PCCT material decomposition (K-channel profile likelihood, Cong 2022), spectral denoising, and virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI + Grant 2014 Mono+) — all dispatching transparently across CPU, Metal, CUDA, and ROCm via AcceleratedKernels.jl.
title: BasisSimulator.jl: Open-source polychromatic CT simulation with a GPU-portable reconstruction stack

summary: Analysis code (code only; no data) for the manuscript "Where are deaths in the Republic of Korea certified with ill-defined causes, and which specific causes are recorded less often there?". Scripts build sex- and age-standardised expected deaths for ill-defined causes of death (ICD-10 R00-R99) in 229 districts, 2011-2024, run pre-specified substitution analyses against specific causes, fit Bayesian negative binomial spatio-temporal models with R-INLA, and generate every number, table and figure in the manuscript. All source statistics are public aggregate data from Statistics Korea and other national sources; processed data are available from the author on reasonable request.
title: Ill-defined causes of death and their inverse relation with specific causes across districts of the Republic of Korea, 2011-2024: analysis code

Traditional materia-medica scholarship is used as a source of research questions, not as a substitute for evidence of human tolerance or cosmetic efficacy. Source-lineage and the native endpoints are inherited from the 817-page STARLI Master Blueprint F111-F115; the narrative and candidate models are newly elaborated research proposals. A five-part chain of source-resolved peptide, carrier and nonclinical evidence F111 - Plant Peptide Extraction Stability at the Limit: primary endpoint sequence-resolved HPLC peptide retention (%). Fair comparator: authenticated free peptide, dark isothermal batch, deoxygenated vehicle and equal-solvent extraction control. Disqualifying counterexample: chromatographic coelution, peptide sequence substitution, oxygen/photo stress confounding and extraction-matrix suppression. F112 - Plant Peptide-Botanical Polyphenol Binding at the Limit: primary endpoint chemically verified peptide-polyphenol bound fraction (%). Fair comparator: free peptide, polyphenol alone, no-polyphenol equal-carrier control and fixed total-solute mixed vehicle. Disqualifying counterexample: irreversible aggregate precipitation, filtration surface loss, fluorescence self-quenching or polymer viscosity artifacts. F113 - Botanical Peptide Nanocarrier Protection at the Limit: primary endpoint parent peptide survival after external protease challenge (%). Fair comparator: free peptide, surface-spiked empty carrier, blank carrier with enzyme, and matched no-enzyme reference. Disqualifying counterexample: inhibited protease masquerading as protection, peptide surface adsorption, incomplete fractionation or analytical recovery loss. F114 - Plant Peptide Enzymatic Degradation Control at the Limit: primary endpoint peptide degradation half-life (h) under a qualified protease assay. Fair comparator: matched protease without carrier, heat-inactivated protease, intact free peptide and equal-matrix blank. Disqualifying counterexample: enzyme inactivation, substrate depletion, product detector saturation, adsorption loss or photochemical decay mistaken for proteolysis. F115 - Skin Compatibility Evidence for Botanical Peptide Blends at the Limit: primary endpoint qualified RhE tissue viability (%) and separately specified irritation surrogate. Fair comparator: vehicle-matched blank, peptide-free carrier, free peptide, polyphenol-free equal carrier and validated irritant reference. Disqualifying counterexample: colored peptide assay interference, tissue nonviability, contact occlusion, vehicle osmolality or cytokine nonspecificity.

summary: BOTANICAL CERAMIDE AND BARRIER-LIPID SCIENCE F106-F110 | Family 22 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch  |  33 x STARLI  |  Edition v1.0 / November 2026 A companion to the 819-page integrated research atlas: botanical-active/ceramide precipitation, three-lipid mole-fraction order, lamellar repeat spacing, spatial delivery and viable-model water-loss evidence. Editorial scope and safety boundary This is a prospective research design, not a report of completed experiments. The graphical response surfaces are synthetic and reproducible. Traditional materia-medica scholarship is used as a source of research questions, not as a substitute for evidence of human tolerance or cosmetic efficacy. Source-lineage and the native endpoints are inherited from the 817-page STARLI Master Blueprint F106-F110; the narrative and candidate models are newly elaborated research proposals. A five-part chain of authenticated botanical, lamellar and barrier evidence F106 - Botanical Active-Ceramide Compatibility at the Limit: primary endpoint botanical-active / ceramide precipitation fraction (%). Fair comparator: full-lipid reference, active-only, ceramide-only, matched vehicle and equal-oil nonlamellar controls. Disqualifying counterexample: color/turbidity interference, precipitated cholesterol, pH-triggered crystal formation, non-specific surface adsorption, pigment scattering. F107 - Ceramide-Cholesterol-Fatty Acid Ratios at the Limit: primary endpoint lamellar-order parameter (dimensionless) under defined three-lipid mole ratios. Fair comparator: matched single-lipid omissions, equimass nonlamellar dispersions and same-total-lipid reference. Disqualifying counterexample: bulk lipid crystallization masquerading as lamellar order, peak overlap, crystal orientation and off-ratio total-solids change. F108 - Botanical Lipid Lamellar Structure Formation at the Limit: primary endpoint lamellar-domain repeat spacing (nm) with reported scattering resolution. Fair comparator: equal-total-lipid disordered reference, reordered lipid mixture and water-activity-matched blank. Disqualifying counterexample: instrument q-calibration drift, sample thickness, cholesterol crystals, preferred orientation or hydration swelling misassigned to layered structure. F109 - Botanical Barrier Lipid Nanodelivery at the Limit: primary endpoint coefficient of variation of component distribution in a nonclinical lipid model (%). Fair comparator: equal-lipid nonlamellar vehicle, matched blank nanocarrier, free-active mixture and depth-attenuation reference. Disqualifying counterexample: fluorescent dye decoupling, light attenuation, optical scatter, surface contamination mistaken for depth deposition. F110 - Barrier Recovery Evidence for Botanical-Ceramide Blends at the Limit: primary endpoint qualified nonclinical water-loss flux (g/m2/h), with independent RhE viability (%). Fair comparator: equal-lipid vehicle, occlusive inert reference, missing-ceramide arm, full-lipid reference and sham-treated qualified RhE. Disqualifying counterexample: temporary occlusive masking, chamber acclimation, humidity drift, damaged or nonviable tissue, incomplete evaporation correction. Methodological introduction Materia-medica provenance without medical overclaim Bencao Gangmu and Chinese materia-medica scholarship inspire questions about material identity, extraction order, mixtures and responsibility for inherited claims. A historical statement cannot determine lipid-layer repeat spacing, chemical compatibility or barrier repair without independent measurement. This volume preserves those sources as research-provoking intellectual history, not proof of efficacy. summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional attention, but rotary position embeddings (RoPE) still confine them to a fixed pretraining window. Existing training-free extrapolation, notably LongLLaDA, copies NTK-based RoPE scaling from autoregressive (AR) models and applies one static, length-only transform at every position and denoising step. That transplant ignores a signal unique to dLLMs: the evolving mask pattern of the partially decoded sequence. We propose Mask-Pattern Position Augmentation (MPPA). MPPA linearly interpolates indices into the pretrained window, then adds a per-position, per-step offset from cumulative mask density. The offset restores rotary phase resolution that interpolation collapses, and it shrinks as tokens are committed, so late steps see near-clean interpolated geometry. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct at twice its 4096-token window, MPPA reduces perplexity from 19.51 under standard decoding to 3.12 at 8192 tokens, below the in-window figure, with 100% passkey retrieval and unchanged needle-in-a-haystack accuracy. These preliminary $2\times$ results motivate mask-conditioned position engineering as a diffusion-native path to long-context generation.
title: Mask-Pattern Position Augmentation: Training-Free Long-Context Extrapolation for Diffusion LLMs

summary: We investigate a failed filament eruption and associated coronal heating in NOAA Active Region 12353 on 2015 May 23, focusing on the relationship between magnetic confinement and external reconnection. Coordinated observations from the Goode Solar Telescope and the Solar Dynamics Observatory, together with nonlinear force-free field extrapolations, allow us to trace the event from the merging of two low-lying filamentary structures to the failed eruption of the resulting elongated filament. Before the rapid rise, the modeled flux rope had entered a regime susceptible to kink instability, while low-atmospheric internal reconnection had already occurred; both may have contributed to the initial acceleration. The rising flux rope remained below the torus instability threshold and was confined by a strong, asymmetric overlying field that compressed it against the overlying loops. An elongated interface brightening, bidirectional plasmoid-like motions, newly brightened loop systems, and progressive weakening of the filament are consistent with external reconnection that changed the magnetic connectivity, removed magnetic flux from the rope, and disrupted its coherent structure. Differential emission measure analysis indicates that the external reconnection heated the active region loop system. A transient, localized structure with high-temperature emission was observed at the interaction interface, consistent with the expected location of a current sheet associated with external reconnection. These results suggest that the strong confining field halted the filament eruption and sustained the interface compression required for current sheet formation, enabling external reconnection to disrupt the flux rope and heat the active region loop system.
title: A Failed Filament Eruption and Associated Active Region Heating Driven by External Magnetic Reconnection

summary: Modelled LGA-week cholera surveillance series for Nigeria, 2022–2024 This dataset contains 120,744 records: 774 Nigerian local government areas (LGAs) across 37 states (36 states and the Federal Capital Territory) and six geopolitical zones, for 156 consecutive epidemiological weeks from 3 January 2022 to 29 December 2024. Each record gives the LGA identifier, name, state and zone, centroid coordinates, a weekly count of suspected cholera cases, and week and year indices. Population denominators come from the 2006 National Population Commission census and are available for 611 of the 774 LGAs (95,316 LGA-weeks). The file also holds simulated covariate columns (water, sanitation and hygiene access, flood risk, temperature, rainfall, mobility, population density and one further parameter) as supplied. Their provenance is undocumented. For selected weeks and states, the file includes state and national cases and deaths transcribed from Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) situation reports. Reproducing the analysis Requires Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas and matplotlib. Put the CSV and the scripts in one folder (or set the environment variable WORKDIR to that folder), then run in this order: exploratory.py, run_chains.py (about four minutes per chain, four chains), post.py, figs12.py, fig3.py. summary: Replication dataset and verification code for the manuscript "Split Custody and Fossilised Provenance: Cross-Regime Recordkeeping Governance Across Space-Mission Closeouts and Schema Migrations". The archive contains 36 unmodified files from the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS3 and PDS4 labels, catalog files, checksum manifests, user guides, errata and node policy pages) for the Apollo 15/17 Heat Flow Experiment, Clementine 1 Bistatic Radar, Magellan Venus GXDR and OSIRIS-REx SPICE archives; a manifest with official URLs and SHA-256 digests for the 10 policy, oversight and case documents analysed in the study (the documents themselves are not redistributed); a dependency-free Python 3 script, run_feasibility_audit.py; and its four output files. Running python3 run_feasibility_audit.py reproduces the output files byte for byte (SHA-256 digests are listed in README_Dataset.md). The script confirms that 11 of 11 PDS4 XML labels are well-formed, inventories 6,378 published MD5 manifest entries (430 in five PDS Geosciences Node manifests and 5,948 in the OSIRIS-REx checksum_v013.tab manifest), matches 22 of 22 local checksum comparisons across 21 sampled files, finds no cryptographic digital signatures in the 36 archive files, and writes the coded evidence matrix (E01 to E10) used in the manuscript. Third-party files in corpus/pds_artifacts/ are redistributed unmodified and remain subject to their original terms. The CC BY 4.0 licence applies to the script, outputs and documentation prepared for this dataset.
title: Replication Dataset and Verification Code for: Split Custody and Fossilised Provenance: Cross-Regime Recordkeeping Governance Across Space-Mission Closeouts and Schema Migrations

summary: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.
title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems

summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in groups, each pursuing an individual objective while jointly determining system performance. If an operator controls which agent observes which other agent, but not their payoffs or messages, how should observations be structured to raise collective welfare? We make the information network (who observes whom) a design object, decoupled from the fixed interaction network over which agents act. Ten identical LLM agents play repeated group-decision games; by default each observes only an anonymous summary of the group's previous-round outcome, and a manager with a fixed budget adds directed observation links that reveal peers' past actions. Across 1,080 episodes and six games spanning coordination, anti-coordination, social dilemmas, and discovery, we ask how much information to share and, at a fixed budget, who should observe whom. Disclosure creates behavioral coupling: observation acts as a contagion channel whose welfare effect depends on the alignment between individually attractive behavior and the collective objective. First, the value of information is alignment-contingent: more peer information tends to help or be neutral when individual behavior is aligned with the collective goal, but under free-riding or congestion externalities it amplifies collectively harmful behavior; in a public-goods game the group does best with no information at all. We read this sign separation as a cross-game regularity within one controlled LLM population, not a model-invariant law. Second, at a fixed budget, who observes whom matters primarily when coupling is harmful: a modular "barbell" that lets sub-populations entrench harmful behavior is reliably the worst wiring, reversing the network-reciprocity intuition from human evolutionary game theory. These results argue against a default of full transparency for agent collectives.
title: Steering Emergent Behavior in Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Information Networks

summary: Effective throughput, the product of raw throughput and transaction success rate, determines the useful capacity of Execute-Order-Validate blockchains such as Hyperledger Fabric. Most prior work either tunes configurations to raise raw throughput, requiring many costly redeployments, or controls conflicts to raise the success rate, repairing them only after execution with kernel modifications. The few joint approaches tune only a small set of parameters and still rely on kernel changes to resolve conflicts. To address these challenges, we present Auriga, a non-invasive framework that jointly optimizes both factors through sample-efficient LLM-guided configuration search and pre-execution conflict prevention. A harness-governed multi-agent architecture coordinates LLM agents for parameter exploration, saturation-aware evaluation, and experience consolidation, with the harness controlling tool and memory access and retaining termination authority. For transaction scheduling, an LLM extracts symbolic AST templates from smart contracts offline. At runtime, the scheduler predicts read-write sets without executing them and partitions transactions into conflict-free groups. Across three benchmarks and conflict rates up to 70%, Auriga improves effective throughput by up to 6.0 times over default Fabric and 2.0 times over the strongest baseline. The tuning agent also discovers undocumented parameter dependencies, and ablation studies show the independent contributions of both subsystems.
title: Auriga: Harness-Governed LLM Agents for Effective Throughput Optimization in Execute-Order-Validate Permissioned Blockchains

summary: Failure attribution in multi-agent systems requires tracing error formation to identify the decisive error step and the responsible agent. However, agents' division of work and information exchange lead to Interleaved Steps and Cluttered Content, requiring models to link executions and check details in lengthy records. This makes it difficult to balance localization accuracy and token cost. We find that multi-agent collaboration also leaves records of how executions connect and content passes between them as results are formed, providing evidence for tracing error formation. Based on this observation, we propose CoLFA (Collaboration-Guided Lightweight Failure Attribution), which uses collaboration cues to organize the attribution input according to how results are formed, determining which steps are examined and how their content is presented. Through Handoff-Guided Step Expansion and Cross-Referenced Content Organization, CoLFA helps the model focus on examining error formation and the role of each decision while reducing the processing of irrelevant and repeated records. Across five settings spanning Who&When and LongRCA and three backbone models, CoLFA achieves the highest exact step-localization accuracy with the lowest token consumption. Compared with individual baselines in each setting, CoLFA improves accuracy by up to 37.50% and reduces token consumption by up to 97.6%.
title: CoLFA: Collaboration-Guided Lightweight Failure Attribution for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Model-based planners that roll out imagined futures assume the transition model faithfully propagates task-relevant signals---a property rarely measured directly. In a single-seed case study of a Recurrent State Space Model world model with active-inference planning in the CARLA driving simulator, we identify a \textbf{posterior-prior gap}---posterior (observation-filtered) states retain obstacle information that imagined rollout states progressively lose: a supervised obstacle probe achieves AUC 0.85 on posterior states, but the same probe applied to imagined prior states shows monotonic decay (AUC 0.85$\rightarrow$0.71 over 15 steps; logit separation drops 57\%). Because the probe is identical, the decay isolates the transition model---not the representation---as the information bottleneck. Obstacle avoidance drops to 0\% without privileged runtime coordinates, and the planner's own ensemble-based epistemic term does not flag the loss---ensemble disagreement yields AUC 0.52 as an obstacle classifier (chance level), making the failure an unflagged imagination failure---an unknown unknown at planning time. As a secondary contribution, we show that \textbf{task-conditioned weighting of Effective Free Energy components} over the same world model yields lane keeping ($81.2 \pm 1.8$\% route completion) and obstacle avoidance (28/28 avoided, \emph{using privileged coordinates}) in the CARLA simulator, with runtime weight modulation enabling post-evasion centering.
title: The Posterior-Prior Epistemic Gap: When World Model Imagination Fails to Carry Task-Relevant Signals

summary: Front-end coding agents are expected to produce applications that fulfill user goals, yet high task scores can coexist with failures in essential workflows. Evaluating these agents therefore requires an explicit distinction between partial implementation and application success. We introduce JoyFrontBench, a benchmark that makes this distinction through goal-oriented acceptance contracts. Each contract identifies core tasks and mandatory criteria before generation: a core task passes only when all mandatory criteria are satisfied and a shared completion threshold is met, while application success requires every core task to pass on the same operational artifact within a single run. Derived from practitioner requirements, JoyFrontBench comprises 100 front-end development problems, 764 tasks, and 2,596 atomic criteria, with reviewed annotations linking user goals to core tasks and evidence requirements. The evaluation framework combines evidence-grounded judgments with deterministic record auditing and fixed scoring rules, preserving graded task assessment alongside explicit core-task and application-level acceptance. We evaluate five coding models under two agent harnesses, OpenHands and OpenCode, on the 70-problem test set; the remaining 30 problems form a public set for validation and diagnostic analyses. Under OpenHands, the mean Average Task Score (ATS) across models is 87.69%, while the mean Application Success Rate (ASR) is 51.52%. Further analyses reveal changes in model rankings across harnesses and variation in application success across repeated runs. These findings highlight the limitations of aggregate task scores in characterizing application success and motivate explicit assessment of core-goal fulfillment alongside graded task performance.
title: JoyFrontBench: Evaluating Front-End Coding Agents through Goal-Oriented Acceptance Contracts

Each contract identifies core tasks and mandatory criteria before generation: a core task passes only when all mandatory criteria are satisfied and a shared completion threshold is met, while application success requires every core task to pass on the same operational artifact within a single run. Derived from practitioner requirements, JoyFrontBench comprises 100 front-end development problems, 764 tasks, and 2,596 atomic criteria, with reviewed annotations linking user goals to core tasks and evidence requirements. The evaluation framework combines evidence-grounded judgments with deterministic record auditing and fixed scoring rules, preserving graded task assessment alongside explicit core-task and application-level acceptance. We evaluate five coding models under two agent harnesses, OpenHands and OpenCode, on the 70-problem test set; the remaining 30 problems form a public set for validation and diagnostic analyses. Under OpenHands, the mean Average Task Score (ATS) across models is 87.69%, while the mean Application Success Rate (ASR) is 51.52%. These findings highlight the limitations of aggregate task scores in characterizing application success and motivate explicit assessment of core-goal fulfillment alongside graded task performance.

summary: Discharge summaries combine a retrospective account of hospitalization with discharge-time decisions. Physician-written references therefore contain both facts supported by prior clinical notes and reference-only content, potentially reflecting clinical synthesis, handoffs, or discharge planning. Reference-only evaluation can conflate failure to recover available information with failure to reproduce content absent from the model input. We introduce FairSumEval, an evidence-aware, fact-level framework that assesses whether each reference and generated fact is supported by the model's evidence and captured by the other summary. The resulting outcome map separates matches, omissions, and additions. Two complementary metrics, Soft IoU-S and Soft IoU-NS, measure reference-generation agreement for facts with and without identified evidence support. On 200 MIMIC-III admissions, 18.8% of physician reference facts have identified support in the prior evidence, compared with 65.4% and 63.5% of facts generated by a general-purpose and a medically specialized model. Overlap is substantially higher for supported content (0.255 and 0.236) than for content without identified support (0.030 and 0.026). The two scores are weakly correlated across admissions (rho = 0.22 and 0.17), and conventional metrics do not consistently capture both dimensions. FairSumEval distinguishes evidence-grounded summarization from agreement on content without identified support, revealing what models omit and add in each category.
title: Discharge Summary Generation Is Not Just Summarization: A Reality Check for Evaluation

summary: Current benchmarks for LLM-driven data agents saturate quickly and cannot target specific capabilities. We present SynthCorp, a platform that creates customizable data estates and benchmarks by simulating how business events produce and modify corporate data over time. Each data estate combines relational databases, a document store, and a data catalog, paired with evaluation tasks and executable gold programs. First, given a scenario and target complexity dimensions, SynthCorp synthesizes reusable event types and compiles each into a program over predefined simulation primitives. Second, SynthCorp schedules event instances on a virtual calendar, interleaving routine and disruption events so that tables, documents, and catalog entries remain consistent. Third, SynthCorp executes the calendar to materialize the data estate and records every operation in a simulation log. Fourth, SynthCorp generates analytical tasks and derives verified gold programs from the log. We use SynthCorp to generate initial evaluation benchmarks comprising seven data estates (up to 1K operational tables) and 256 tasks across five domains. The data estates pass deterministic pipeline checks (such as foreign-key violations, undeclared writes, recurrence violations, and database execution failures) with a near-zero error rate, introduce cross-asset complexities, and cover all requested dimensions. Evaluating three models across four data-context settings shows that the benchmarks separate data contexts and model tiers. Auditing candidate queries against causal provenance in the simulation log verifies gold programs without manual annotation, including on multi-event composite tasks that expose reasoning failures in state-of-the-art agents. We hope the community uses SynthCorp to generate more challenging and useful data estates and benchmarks that foster the development of enterprise data agents.
title: SynthCorp: A Platform for Creating Benchmarks for Data Agents

summary: We show that cyclic fatigue can occur in a system whose elements behave elastically up to an irreversible failure threshold, without plasticity, friction, or any time-dependent process. The model represents a weak interface between two elastic bodies loaded in shear. Under sufficiently large cyclic loading below the static failure threshold, a pre-existing flaw advances progressively, by a few lattice spacings per cycle. Two conditions are needed for this behavior: each bond fails more easily under one sense of the shear than the opposite, and the shear must be reversed during the cycle by an amount large enough to break bonds that have not yet failed. The model thus identifies the minimal conditions for an intrinsic, plasticity-free fatigue mechanism. Such conditions may be met at interfaces and weak planes subjected to strongly reversed shear, as in fretting, rolling contact, and reversed torsion, or in cyclic shear of cemented granular materials.
title: Fatigue crack growth without plasticity under cyclically reversed shear

Paediatric age group along with various syndromes like VACTREL association in combination with laparoscopic approach for the correction of ARM pose unique challenges to anaesthesiologists, of which the presence of spinal dysraphism is particularly important as the analgesia in paediatric age group relies on neuraxial techniques like caudal block. Furthermore, providing adequate and sustained perioperative analgesia can be challenging due to the prolonged duration of surgery, involvement of both abdominal and perineal surgical fields, and limitations associated with conventional single-shot neuraxial techniques. ARMs are also the leading cause of intestinal obstruction in the neonatal period in most of the lower-middle income countries in the world [2]. The incidence may be as high as 2.54 per 10,000 cases in middle income countries due to lower registered birth defects. As a famous Anecdote by Dr WJ Potts says “a properly functioning rectum is an unappreciated gift of the greatest price,” holds true in terms of ARM as well. summary: Autonomous cyber defense is widely studied with deep reinforcement learning, but most work trains policies inside simulators because learning requires many trial-and-error interactions. Simulator-based training carries a fidelity gap: trained policies face authentication delays, partial action failures, service dependencies, and user traffic patterns that the simulator did not represent, and degrade on transfer. Training directly in the network being defended removes the gap but makes every interaction slow and costly, so sample efficiency becomes the binding constraint. Model-based reinforcement learning has reduced sample requirements on games and physical robots by orders of magnitude by planning inside a learned world model, but it has not been applied to defenders trained in operational networks. We present FOE-Dreamer (Factored Opponent-Enhanced Dreamer), a model-based reinforcement learning framework that trains a defender online and directly in a network on cloud infrastructure, without a simulator stage. FOE-Dreamer separates three sources of variation in the latent state: a controllable component driven by defender actions, an exogenous component driven by benign user activity, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable signals alone. Separating the components reduces the variance in policy gradients during planning in imagination. Against two scripted attacker profiles with user activity emulated by the GHOSTS framework on an 8-host OpenStack testbed, FOE-Dreamer trains within a 3-day budget on a single GPU and achieves about 2$\times$ better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN baselines under matched compute. Both the factoring and the opponent model contribute to the gain, and the learned latents are consistent with the intended separation.
title: FOE-Dreamer: Deployment-Efficient Learning of Cyber Defense Policies in Operational Networks

summary: The visual world is cluttered: robust vision-language reasoning requires ignoring irrelevant information. Yet vision-language models (VLMs) can suffer substantial accuracy losses when answering questions about a target image with distractors present. Existing mitigations focus on selecting relevant images or limiting information exchange between images. Through a systematic analysis of three open 7-8B VLMs on five perception benchmarks adapted to include distractor images, we show that distractors reduce accuracy even when models correctly identify the relevant image, suggesting that selection alone is not enough. To understand the mechanism behind this interference, we combine attention analysis with targeted knockouts in Qwen2.5-VL and identify middle-layer distractor-to-text connections as a pathway through which irrelevant visual information affects reasoning. We introduce answer consistency regularization, which encourages consistent answer distributions with and without distractors. Without directly constraining attention, this objective reduces middle-layer attention from question tokens to distractor images, consistent with the pathway our analysis implicates. With five distractors, our approach improves circular accuracy by an average of 16 percentage points over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline across the five benchmarks while preserving single-image performance.
title: Back to the Question: Tracing Visual Distraction Through Text Tokens

summary: Strongly correlated topological states in Kondo lattices represent a frontier in condensed matter physics, where the coupling between boundary electrons and localized f states can reshape the low-energy electronic structure. Here, we combine termination-resolved angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), Ce 4$d \rightarrow 4f$ resonant photoemission, and surface electronic structure calculations to investigate the Kondo lattice compound CeCuAs$_2$. Two distinct surface electronic structures are assigned to the As1 and CeAs2 terminations through their characteristic Fermi-surface geometries and termination-specific calculations. On CeAs2, a Dirac surface state associated with the calculated nontrivial bulk topology coexists with a weakly dispersive Ce 4$f$ band near $E_F$. Resonant photoemission identifies the low-energy 4$f$ character and reveals crystal-field-related fine structure in the energy range traversed by the Dirac branch. On cooling, the 4$f$ and Dirac regions both gain spectral weight, whereas a reference conduction-band region changes much less. Together, these observations provide spectroscopic evidence for termination-selective $f$-Dirac hybridization and the development of 4$f$ character in a topological surface state. Our results identify surface termination as a microscopic means of controlling the interplay between Kondo correlations and topological boundary electrons.
title: Termination-selective Kondo hybridization of topological surface states in CeCuAs$_2$

summary: Reward models (RMs) are increasingly deployed as service components in LLM alignment pipelines, where payment, audit, moderation, and governance workflows act on the scores they return. An inference proof alone does not show whether a score belongs to the intended request, model checkpoint, numerical configuration, and verifier: in a controlled comparison that isolates the accepted statement from prover scale, a generic inference proof wrapped for on-chain checking remains valid after six classes of such service-field substitution. We formulate verifiable reward-model-as-a-service (VRMaaS) as a service-output integrity problem and present a framework in which each returned reward becomes a proof-carrying artifact. Its off-chain acceptance rule binds request identity, committed weights, verifier and configuration identifiers, proof-task order, and the digest of the exported package, so auditors can check a reward without rerunning the private RM or exposing inputs, checkpoints, or hidden activations; an optional on-chain zero-knowledge wrapper gives contracts a partial attestation of selected consistency checks and supplied service fields. The framework decomposes Transformer RM serving into arithmetic and lookup-backed proof tasks, aggregates them into a composite proof, and links hidden operands to the committed weights. A GPU prototype on 1B, 3B, and 8B reward models over 128-1024 tokens preserves 93.5-99% pairwise agreement with the baseline RM and rejects every tested service-field substitution in complete artifacts. Using exact integer witnesses and request-level aggregation of weight-binding openings, it generates complete artifacts in 49.8-206.1 seconds across the evaluated settings; auditors verify retained artifacts in 1.94-5.11 seconds, and partial public attestation costs about 217K gas. These costs suit delayed audit, settlement, and governance workflows.
title: VRMaaS: Verifiable Reward-Model-as-a-Service for Trustworthy LLM Alignment

summary: Parallel test-time scaling (TTS) has been shown to enhance reasoning in large language models by generating and aggregating multiple independent reasoning paths. Internal confidence scores can further improve this process by identifying paths of varying quality. However, existing methods remain computationally inefficient, as low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated. In this work, we aim to improve the use of internal confidence signals for better model performance and computational efficiency. We begin by offering a new perspective on the role of confidence in aggregation, showing that it is most impactful for questions near the decision boundary. Notably, when amplified by multi-sample aggregation, even small confidence signals derived from short prefixes can meaningfully influence outcomes in these boundary cases. Building on this insight, we introduce Prefix-Guided Sampling (PreG), a method that reallocates computation by first generating short prefixes, ranking them using internal confidence scores, and then completing only the most promising candidates. This strategy reduces token usage while maintaining gains in path quality. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that, under a fixed compute budget, PreG strengthens the effective signal by widening the decision boundary margin. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms standard parallel TTS approaches across benchmarks, while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.
title: Early Signals, Strong Decisions: Prefix-Guided Sampling for Parallel Test-Time Scaling

summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an integral part of wireless systems, yet much of today's wireless AI remains task-specific and reactive, with models typically trained to map current observations to predefined outputs or reconstruct observed data. While effective for individual tasks, such approaches provide limited support for learning what is predictable, reusable, and transferable in dynamic wireless environments. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) offers a different perspective by learning predictive representations in latent space that capture informative structure in the observations. In this article, we introduce Communication JEPA (CommJEPA) as a communication-oriented framework for predictive representation learning. The central idea is bidirectional. JEPA can equip wireless systems with predictive representations for capturing latent channel and environmental dynamics, integrating heterogeneous observations, adapting to changing conditions, and supporting future decisions. Conversely, the physical structure, partial observability, multiple time scales, action-dependent evolution, and resource constraints of wireless systems motivate new communication-aware JEPA designs. We develop this mutual perspective, organize the resulting design space, and discuss representative JEPA-based wireless instantiations for prediction and control. We further highlight open challenges toward scalable, interactive, and predictive wireless intelligence.
title: CommJEPA: When Predictive Representation Learning Meets Wireless Intelligence

JEPA can equip wireless systems with predictive representations for capturing latent channel and environmental dynamics, integrating heterogeneous observations, adapting to changing conditions, and supporting future decisions. Conversely, the physical structure, partial observability, multiple time scales, action-dependent evolution, and resource constraints of wireless systems motivate new communication-aware JEPA designs. We develop this mutual perspective, organize the resulting design space, and discuss representative JEPA-based wireless instantiations for prediction and control. We further highlight open challenges toward scalable, interactive, and predictive wireless intelligence.
title: CommJEPA: When Predictive Representation Learning Meets Wireless Intelligence

summary: Unfamiliar walkers may follow the shortest route and miss nearby shade, indoor passages and multilevel connections. We define the resulting hidden solar cost as the direct-sun exposure avoidable through shade-informed routing without substantial detours. We developed a time-specific three-dimensional model of Hong Kong Island that combines indoor and outdoor walking networks with building geometry, vegetation mapped by light detection and ranging (LiDAR), and solar position. For 500 modelled journeys, we compared shortest and shade-informed routes at four daytime snapshots and five extra-distance limits. At noon, shade-informed routes reduced modelled direct-sun exposure by 13.5% relative to shortest routes under a 10% extra-distance limit. Route length increased by 2.85% on average. A 5% extra-distance limit delivered 77% of the reduction obtained at 10%. In a controlled comparison, outdoor shade information accounted for 86% of the reduction and indoor-protection information for 14%. Removing multilevel connections left only 191 of 500 journeys feasible within the original route-length limit. These route comparisons identify an avoidable solar cost when existing protection is missing from the information used to choose a route. Making protected routes visible and preserving their connections can reduce sun exposure without large detours.
title: The hidden solar cost of urban unfamiliarity

summary: Heat dissipation in laser optical materials depends not only on their thermal conductivity but also on how absorbed energy is redistributed among various phonon modes. In calcium fluoride (CaF2), rapid energy transfer from hot electrons to weakly propagating longitudinal optical (LO) phonons can create a nonequilibrium phonon bottleneck effect that limits efficient heat removal. Here, we propose selective phonon excitation as an effective strategy to break this bottleneck. Combining electron-phonon scattering calculations, phonon Boltzmann transport analysis, and nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations, we identify LO phonons as the primary modes that preferentially receive energy from hot carriers, leading to energy accumulation due to their inefficient transport and relaxation. Guided by three-phonon scattering phase-space analysis, selective excitation of transverse acoustic (TA) modes can accelerate LO relaxation and promote energy transfer toward heat-carrying acoustic modes. While sustained LO-phonon excitation reduces the thermal conductivity by approximately 12%, additional TA-mode excitation improves heat conduction by approximately 21% compared to the state limited by the LO-phonon bottleneck, surpassing the unexcited value. These findings demonstrate that controlling interbranch energy redistribution can counteract phonon-bottleneck-induced heat accumulation and reveal a working route for active thermal management in laser optical materials through selective control of phonon populations.
title: Improving Nonequilibrium Thermal Conduction in CaF2 by Breaking the Phonon Bottleneck Effect

summary: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.
title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving

summary: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. The measured effect is spatially concentrated at 7-8B and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in the tested 32B configuration. In dual-path unified models (BAGEL, Janus-Pro), the causal handle localizes to the generation pathway as a compact one-dimensional carrier. The understanding pathway also encodes spatial information in a higher-rank, probe-decodable form, but is not the causal handle. To separate decodability from causal use, we analyze concentration, alignment, and semantic location. These diagnostics explain why behavior, probing, and intervention can diverge. Multimodal training thus reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, not just how visual input is processed.
title: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training
