summary: Data and result logs of the PhishVN URL-benchmark study: the three external corpora in the exact rows the study used, and (from version 1.2.0) the study's result logs. External corpora. Class-balanced 1:1 subsamples of PhiUSIIL (20,000 rows, UCI, label polarity converted so that 1 is phishing), ISCX-URL2016 (15,894 rows) and PhishStorm (20,000 rows), the last two in the phishing/legitimate form redistributed with the GramBeddings repository. Each row carries the host the study featurises, 25 lexical features in the CompPhish schema (computed with the public-suffix list of the library version used) and the label. The subsamples were not drawn by a seed, so these files define the transfer experiments. With the PhishVN corpus (Mendeley Data, DOI 10.17632/b97hxbxtpd.4) they are the inputs of the benchmark, protocol, decomposition and transfer tables, which the walkthrough notebook notebooks/url_benchmark/url_benchmark_walkthrough.ipynb in https://github.com/vuthainguyen1602/phishvn recomputes. Cite the original datasets when using the rows (see README.md). Result logs ( results.zip ). One row per model family, protocol and seed for every experiment, the summary files the paper's tables are generated from, and the logs of the analyses added in the first revision (operating points, forward cut-offs, label-error scenarios, corpus probe, two-class temporal check, string models, tuning, attribution, cost). results_manifest.csv inside the archive gives every file's size and SHA-256. The files are aggregates and hold no URL, hostname or e-mail address. Three files of the repository's results folder are not included because they are copies of corpus rows (the PhishVN corpus one row per URL or per host); they are regenerated from the public corpus by the scripts the repository names. Files: phiusiil_compphish.csv , iscx_compphish.csv , phishstorm_compphish.csv , results.zip , README.md , SHA256SUMS . Version 1.2.0 adds results.zip ; the three data files are byte-identical to versions 1.0.0 and 1.1.0.
title: PhishVN URL benchmark: the external transfer corpora and the study's result logs

summary: Version 3 — published 13 November 2026. This release includes the GB1 model-identity correction described below. This archive contains the manuscript-adopted results supporting the evaluation of full-parameter domain-specific unsupervised fine-tuning (DS-UFT) of ESM-2 650M. It includes sequence pseudo-perplexity, contact prediction, secondary-structure prediction and GB1 mutational-effect prediction results, adopted supplementary controls, confidence intervals, figure assets, executable analysis code and SHA-256 file manifests. GB1 results use validation-selected configurations; unused exploratory and test-selected alternatives are excluded. The archive includes 85 adopted checkpoint files: 30 secondary-structure heads, five L2 contact heads, 35 frozen-representation GB1 heads and 15 GB1 SFT trainable-parameter checkpoints. Full pretrained/DS-UFT backbone checkpoints and complete third-party databases are not bundled; verified external backbone references and loading requirements are provided. Model-identity correction: The two adopted mean-pooled GB1 conditions previously labeled PF00076_05 and PF00076_09 actually used PF00067_05 and PF00067_09. Checkpoint hashes and direct embedding reproduction verified the identity. Corresponding labels, Figure S7, head paths and backbone references are corrected; predictions, performance estimates, confidence intervals and fitted weight bytes are unchanged. The two affected candidate-corpus overlap comparisons are recomputed using the correct PF00067 collections. Genuine PF00076 experiments in other tasks are unaffected. See the archive provenance for scope and limitations. This release supports reconstruction of the included results, not end-to-end reproduction of every historical training workflow. Code: DS-UFT-Benchmark . Version-series DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23045593 .

summary: Indoor air quality and maintenance of plants very important but often overlooked factors in today’s living spaces. This paper is proposing Project P.A.S.O (Plant-Assisted Smart Organizer). an innovative and eco-friendly solution for indoor air purification and soil moisture detection. Using an experimental research approach, this study examines the efficacy of a special clay pot with activated charcoal and hydrochromic and thermochromic paints. The main objective of this study is to find out the best ratio of activated charcoal and the clay material by taking 50 g, 100 g, and 150 g of activated charcoal per 1.5 kg of clay to obtain maximum stability against Total Volatile Organic Compounds (TVOCs) and particulate matter. Moreover, the application of hydrochromic and thermochromic technology allows creating a non-electronic, visual feedback system that changes color depending on the hydration and temperature status of the soil, thus solving the problem of abandonment of plants or their watering. The data was collected through controlled testing of air quality and standardized observation checklists to test the accuracy of pollutant removal and color change detection. The results reveal that the combination of the carbon-treated clay mixture significantly improves air filtration performance compared to conventional earthenware while the color-coding system can be used as a reliable and low-cost alternative to expensive digital sensors. By combining traditional pottery with modern material science, Project P.A.S.O provides a sustainable and decorative household tool that promotes healthier indoor climates and enhances urban gardening practices. The study concludes that this biomimetic method is a viable approach that can be used to counter indoor pollution and promote plant health without the need for any external power source.
title: Project P.A.S.O: A Plant-Assisted Smart Organizer for Air-Purification and Soil Moisture Monitoring

summary: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablations identify and validate two recurring design patterns: retaining raw conversations as retrievable evidence preserves details omitted from extracted memories, while composing retrieved evidence according to query intent helps the answering model use it effectively. Transplanting the composition module into five existing memory systems improves accuracy across all five. Beyond these patterns, the search objective shapes where computation goes: optimizing serving cost alongside accuracy shifts computation from LLM-based memory construction to selective processing at query time while retaining competitive accuracy. Together, these findings offer empirical lessons for agent memory design. Code is available at https://github.com/ash-ding/MAPE.
title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution

summary: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.
title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video

summary: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam
title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP

summary: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.
title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning

summary: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.
title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination

summary: Long-term spacecraft autonomy requires embodied agents to use operational history under communication delays, time-critical operations, environmental uncertainty, complex physical interactions, power and computational constraints, and safety and reliability requirements. We introduce AstroMemBench and a Scenario-Challenge-Capability design method that maps these requirements to executable memory tests. The benchmark covers 16 memory subchallenges through 140 templates and 2240 instances across nine tasks in planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration. A deterministic environment scores actions for task completion, state changes, safety, and resource use. Ablations under nine conditions show that the benchmark is sensitive to how accurately agents recover and use historical information and to differences in memory-system design. Main experiments compare six configurations. Mem0, Chain-of-Memory, LightMem, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve same-session mean scores over native Pi Agent, with no clear advantage of the three memory systems over RAG. After a session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points. Benefits favor instruction retention and result reuse over ongoing state tracking and energy reservation. AstroMemBench supports the design, development, and selection of memory systems for embodied spacecraft agents. AstroMemBench 1.0 and its evaluation code are publicly available: https://github.com/flyingView/AstroMemBench-v1.
title: AstroMemBench: A Benchmark for Memory Systems in Embodied Spacecraft Agents

summary: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.
title: PhysCapBench: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Physically Grounded Video Captioning

summary: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.
title: Beyond Compressing Everything: Contrastive Memory Learning for Selective Context Compression

summary: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.

summary: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.
title: Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents

summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models through forward-only evaluations, but high-dimensional random perturbations can limit optimization efficiency. Sparse perturbations reduce the search dimension, making the selection of informative coordinates critical. We propose Wanda-Importance Sparsity-MeZO (WIS-MeZO), which uses Wanda weight--activation saliency to construct task-conditioned sparse perturbation masks while keeping the pretrained model dense. We analyze support quality through gradient energy capture and relate it to gradient estimation and convergence. Across 16 benchmarks with LLaMA and Qwen models ranging from 3B to 32B parameters, WIS-MeZO achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and reaches comparable validation losses in fewer optimization steps. Comparisons with random and magnitude-based sparse perturbations further highlight the importance of informative support selection.
title: Wanda-Guided Sparse Perturbations for Efficient Zeroth-Order Optimization

summary: We explore the use of AI agents for solving computational problems in algebra. For the problems we consider, the main challenge is not correctness but \emph{time}: general-purpose algorithms are guaranteed to provide correct solutions but can be prohibitively slow, while reformulations that exploit special structure often allow solving a problem much faster. We propose to use this setting to evaluate how effectively agents discover and exploit structure within and across tasks to reduce computational costs. More broadly, computational algebra supplies infinitely many problems with independently verifiable answers and systematically controllable structure and difficulty. To illustrate these possibilities, we use benchmark families of systems with controlled shared structure and evaluate agents in three settings: solving independent instances, solving online streams of related instances using persistent memory, and compiling a fast reusable solver for a known problem family. Our experiments show that (i) agents can extend the range of systems solvable within a fixed budget, although reasoning overhead can sometimes outweigh computational savings; (ii) memory can reduce the cost of repeated solving but may preserve suboptimal strategies; (iii) compilation produces faster reusable solvers but at substantial upfront cost. Overall, computational algebra offers concrete, measurable targets for improving how agents discover and reuse structure.
title: Agentic Computational Algebra

summary: Analog in-memory computing offers the potential to accelerate approximate inverse preconditioning, but hardware errors can degrade preconditioners designed in digital arithmetic. We develop an analog-digital preconditioner for symmetric positive-definite linear systems that combines analog block Jacobi with a small digital low-rank residual correction. The correction space is constructed by probing the same programmed analog arrays used in the solve, targeting errors from both the coupling omitted by block Jacobi and persistent hardware perturbations. Under a random linear-operator model, we separate the programmed-mean error from fresh read fluctuations, distinguish the effects of copy averaging and repeated reads, and quantify the sampling accuracy of columnwise probing. Under a centered additive write-noise model, we also derive a computable regularization threshold and identify the approximation error introduced by the regularization shift. Experiments with an analog hardware simulator show that programming errors can change the directions that block Jacobi reduces poorly. In the tested comparisons with significant programming errors, learning the correction space from the programmed copies reduces FGMRES iteration counts relative to construction from digital block Jacobi.
title: Noise-Adaptive Analog-Digital Preconditioning

summary: We study recovery of an initial state from dynamical samples of a trajectory driven by unknown additive forcing. Measurements against both the original sensors and their images under the adjoint nominal evolution yield one-step residuals that cancel the initial state exactly. These residuals separate forcing estimation from initial-state reconstruction. For a centered Gaussian forcing model with fixed covariance parameters, we combine Gaussian conditioning with canonical dual-frame reconstruction and derive an exact unconditional second-moment identity, including the correlation between the forcing-estimation error and the measurement noise. We also obtain high-probability bounds and identify the irreducible forcing uncertainty through a conditional covariance in the geometry induced by the prior. A hierarchy of augmented sensor systems separates the role of sampling depth in forcing visibility from that of the observation horizon in nominal observability. An image-transport experiment and finite-dimensional and periodic-convolution experiments illustrate the residual correction and the separate roles of sampling depth and observation horizon.
title: Augmented Dynamical Sampling under unmodeled Forcing

summary: Can the spatial correlations of a quantum environment be revealed through work extraction? We address this question using two harmonic-oscillator detectors coupled to either an accelerated vacuum or a matched inertial thermal field. We establish a quantitative connection between the spatial correlations of the environment and the equilibrium Gaussian ergotropy, showing that the leading extractable work is governed by a response-weighted spatial correlation. Although the two environments have identical local spectra, their different spatial correlations give rise to distinct work responses. We further identify a finite-distance blind point at which a single measurement configuration fails to distinguish the two environments. By reversing the direct coupling between the detectors, we develop a two-setting scheme that removes this ambiguity and reconstructs the underlying spatial correlations from work measurements. This reconstruction remains effective beyond the weak-coupling regime. We also show that spatial correlations can provide additional global work even when the detector pair is separable, demonstrating that entanglement is not a necessary resource for this advantage. Finally, we investigate the transient evolution of Gaussian ergotropy and reveal its oscillatory decay and dependence on acceleration and detector parameters. Our results establish Gaussian ergotropy as an operational probe of spatial correlations in bosonic environments.
title: Gaussian ergotropy and spatial correlations: accelerated vacuum versus a thermal field

summary: Patient-specific airway modelling requires geometrically consistent lumen surfaces with identifiable boundaries and support for controlled anatomical modifications. We present CT-RespGeomLib, a deterministic framework that converts CT airway masks into two complementary representations: an editable assembly of semantically labelled pipe and junction blocks connected through canonical shared ports, and a fused lumen surface reconstructed from tapered implicit primitives with validated port-to-boundary loop correspondence. The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.
title: CT-RespGeomLib: Deterministic reconstruction of CT airway masks into editable,port-matched lumen geometry

summary: SignalAudit-QD is a reproducible audit resource for testing whether a dated public signal adds information beyond query history in a fixed 20-term U.S. AI panel. It aligns two archived Google Trends extractions with eight USPTO AI-patent publication streams and releases origin-indexed predictions, paired losses, provenance, executable tests, and tamper-evident run manifests. Both inputs are retrospective reconstructions obtained after the modeled 2020--2023 origins; the task is therefore a pseudo-origin assay within frozen measurement vintages, not a historical deployment simulation. In the designated one-month comparison, adding a two-component patent block to a level ridge changes macro mean absolute error by +0.0012 Trends points, with conditional 95% moving-block interval [-0.0363,+0.0387]. This establishes neither aggregate benefit nor equivalence. Alternative dimensions, semantic mapping, patent definitions, a second extraction, and a three-month horizon remain unresolved; persistence-anchored and nonlinear hosts instead show model-specific worsening, tiny for the anchored fit. Matched timing controls expose availability assumptions, while a planted-signal assay detects only the largest tested injection. A within-query high-interest alert demonstrates the released interface but not online utility. The contribution is a bounded negative case study and an extensible evidence schema for auditing external-signal claims in temporal information retrieval.
title: SignalAudit-QD: A Reproducible Audit Resource for External Signals in AI-Query Forecasting

summary: Gravitational-wave observations have opened new opportunities to study massive object events like merging binary black holes. When combined with electromagnetic counterparts, accurate localization of gravitational-wave sources could allow us to identify their host galaxies and carry out follow-up studies, such as study the environment of merging black holes and determine the Hubble constant. One of the possible methods for precise localization is strong gravitational-wave lensing. Previous studies have considered strong gravitational-wave lensing with galaxy lenses. However, galaxy clusters have yet to be investigated due to the complexity of their mass structures. Here we take the list of known cluster lenses from the Hubble Frontier Fields, simulate lensing properties of gravitational waves from their reconstructions as they would be observed by the ground-based gravitational-wave detectors. When same model family is used in simulation and localization, we find that the correct lens is identified for around 90\% of the simulated events. We also show that the source positions within the cluster can be pinpointed at sub-arcsecond precision with an estimate on source redshift. When we marginalize over all possible lens models for the clusters, the lens identification and localizations remain valid as long as the correct lens model is contained in the available cluster lens models. However, most localization attempts fail at initialization if the correct cluster model is excluded. These tests establish a proof of concept of localization under idealized conditions, while more work is needed to understand the cluster lens modeling discrepancies and reconstruction bias to validate the approach further.
title: Localization of gravitational-wave source behind galaxy clusters by gravitational-wave lensing

summary: This paper investigates the global geometry of loxodromes and loxodromic curves on surfaces of revolution in $\mathbb{R}^3$. A loxodrome is a regular curve avoiding the poles and making a constant directed angle with the meridians. To allow curves to reach or pass through poles, we introduce loxodromic curves, whose pole-free interior portions are loxodromes. The directed azimuths of these portions agree modulo $π$. We classify surfaces of revolution into four types based on the number of poles and whether the profile curve is closed: cylinder-like, torus-like, paraboloid-like, and sphere-like. For cylinder-like surfaces, every maximal loxodromic curve other than a parallel is non-self-intersecting. For torus-like surfaces, nonparallel maximal loxodromic curves are closed or dense according to the rationality of their rotation numbers. For paraboloid-like and sphere-like surfaces, only maximal meridians can pass smoothly through poles, while nonmeridional, nonparallel maximal loxodromic curves have poles as endpoints. We derive the differential equations for arc-length-parametrized loxodromes and introduce coordinates in which they are represented by straight lines. We solve the direct and inverse problems for loxodromic segments on all four surface types and give criteria for maximal loxodromic curves to be geodesics. We show that diffeomorphisms preserving maximal loxodromic curves preserve surface type and that their inverses preserve such curves. These maps preserve maximal meridians and parallels on surfaces with poles, but need not do so on pole-free surfaces. We characterize azimuth-consistent diffeomorphisms and, for cylinder-like surfaces, establish criteria for conformality and isometry. In particular, azimuth-consistent diffeomorphisms are conformal when both surfaces have poles.
title: Classification and Geometry of Loxodromic Curves on Surfaces of Revolution in Three-Dimensional Euclidean Space

summary: Machine learning coupled with device simulation is widely used to optimize thin-film solar cells, but almost exclusively in the forward direction, from device parameters to predicted performance. The inverse problem encountered after fabrication, namely identifying the mechanism that limits a given device, is still addressed by manual inspection of characterization data. In this work, both directions are examined for lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells using approximately 42,000 SCAPS-1D simulations. Replacing the Spiro-OMeTAD hole transport layer with CuI increases the simulated power conversion efficiency from 19.6\% to 21.6\%, almost entirely through the fill factor. Surrogate models trained and tested on a factorial parameter grid substantially overstate their predictive accuracy. An XGBoost regressor attains $R^2 = 0.9997$ on held-out grid points but only 0.58 on independently sampled devices, whereas training on a Latin hypercube design of comparable size restores $R^2 = 0.995$. For the inverse problem, a multi-label classifier identifies which of six degradation mechanisms are present from simulated temperature- and illumination-dependent open-circuit-voltage measurements. It achieves a macro $F_1$ score of 0.938, compared to 0.687 for a calibrated physics-rule baseline. The classifier does not, however, generalize to combinations of mechanisms absent from the training set.
title: Interpretable machine learning diagnosis of degradation mechanisms in lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells from temperature- and illumination-dependent electrical measurements

summary: Accurate photometric-redshift estimation and calibration of the weak-lensing point-spread function (PSF) for Euclid require complementary ground-based optical imaging with high photometric precision and spatial homogeneity. The Organisation Unit for External Data (OU-EXT) integrates heterogeneous ground-based surveys into the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), delivering uniformly calibrated, co-added images, and associated PSF models. To minimise systematics in spectral energy distribution (SED) reconstruction and photometric-redshift estimation, these data must achieve relative photometric stability at the $\sim$10 mmag level on Euclid-tile scales. We present the ground-based imaging component of Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), comprising $\sim2500$ deg$^2$ across the wide, deep, and auxiliary fields. We summarise the OU-EXT production workflow and validation framework, and quantify the achieved data quality of the co-added products in terms of depth, photometric zero-point stability, and spatial colour homogeneity. In the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the point-source $10σ$ depths in the $griz$ bands reach 24.8/24.3/24.0/23.0 AB mag, with the deep fields extending 1--2 magnitudes deeper. Most EWS DR1 tiles meet the 10 mmag relative photometric requirement, with 1.1% and 1.5% showing offsets exceeding 50 mmag in the northern and southern hemispheres, respectively. Spatial colour variations remain typically below 5--10 mmag across the southern EWS footprint, while larger residual structures of 10--25 mmag appear in some northern regions. These results demonstrate that the EXT production chain provides a largely homogeneous framework for integrating ground-based datasets into Euclid, while identifying calibration and co-addition limitations that have to be addressed in DR2 to meet the mission's most stringent cosmological requirements. (Abridged)

summary: Accurate photometric-redshift estimation and calibration of the weak-lensing point-spread function (PSF) for Euclid require complementary ground-based optical imaging with high photometric precision and spatial homogeneity. The Organisation Unit for External Data (OU-EXT) integrates heterogeneous ground-based surveys into the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), delivering uniformly calibrated, co-added images, and associated PSF models. To minimise systematics in spectral energy distribution (SED) reconstruction and photometric-redshift estimation, these data must achieve relative photometric stability at the $\sim$10 mmag level on Euclid-tile scales. We present the ground-based imaging component of Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), comprising $\sim2500$ deg$^2$ across the wide, deep, and auxiliary fields. We summarise the OU-EXT production workflow and validation framework, and quantify the achieved data quality of the co-added products in terms of depth, photometric zero-point stability, and spatial colour homogeneity. In the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the point-source $10σ$ depths in the $griz$ bands reach 24.8/24.3/24.0/23.0 AB mag, with the deep fields extending 1--2 magnitudes deeper. Most EWS DR1 tiles meet the 10 mmag relative photometric requirement, with 1.1% and 1.5% showing offsets exceeding 50 mmag in the northern and southern hemispheres, respectively. Spatial colour variations remain typically below 5--10 mmag across the southern EWS footprint, while larger residual structures of 10--25 mmag appear in some northern regions. These results demonstrate that the EXT production chain provides a largely homogeneous framework for integrating ground-based datasets into Euclid, while identifying calibration and co-addition limitations that have to be addressed in DR2 to meet the mission's most stringent cosmological requirements. summary: CREAM v1.1 provides an ensemble reconstruction of East Asian summer monsoon circulation for May–September 1855–1907, constrained by monthly wet-day counts from the historical Seoul Cheugugi rain-gauge record through offline ensemble data assimilation. The dataset contains frozen prior and posterior ensemble-mean anomaly fields for sea-level pressure (SLP), 850-hPa geopotential height (Z850), and zonal and meridional winds (U850 and V850) on a global T42 grid (64 latitudes × 128 longitudes), together with point-wise posterior ensemble standard deviations. Anomalies are referenced to the historical ensemble’s own 1855–1907 monthly climatology. A separate file, CREAM_v1.1_prior_members.nc , provides the ten GOGA prior ensemble members used in the reconstruction as full fields, together with this reference climatology. These allow users to examine the prior ensemble and recover model-referenced absolute prior and posterior mean fields on valid grid cells. The package also includes the western North Pacific subtropical high (WNPSH) western-edge index, per-year 5 × 5 monthly index covariance matrices, monthly Z850 reliability grades, historical and modern observation records, a provenance-based observation-error budget, assimilation feedback, and verification results. The assimilated historical wet-day counts incorporate eight adjudicated daily readings supplied with the observations. Python production, analysis, and figure-generation scripts, numerical figure inputs, four worked examples, and reproducibility documentation are provided. Posterior field-level ensemble members and full field covariance matrices are not included. CREAM v1.1 is a weakly constrained reconstruction intended primarily for WNPSH-index, seasonal, and epoch-scale analyses. In the development-exposed 2015–2024 modern holdout, near-Korea monthly Z850 root-mean-square error (RMSE), evaluated against NCEP/NCAR R1, improves by 1.6% relative to the SST-forced prior (95% confidence interval: +0.4 to +2.7%), although absolute monthly-field RMSE remains above climatology. The supplied reliability grades assess improvement over the prior for specified monthly Z850 composites within the East Asian evaluation domain; they do not certify absolute accuracy, other variables, or seasonal and epoch averages. May–June monthly fields are not recommended for use. WNPSH seasonal uncertainty derived from the supplied monthly covariance matrices represents conditional ensemble uncertainty and does not include stationarity or model-structure errors. Development exposure and recommended-use limitations are documented in the accompanying materials. The supplied numerical inputs support manuscript-figure rendering and selected verification and confidence-interval calculations without rerunning the full assimilation. The fourth worked example checks the released prior ensemble against the frozen product and reproduces a selected year’s assimilation update over the WNPSH Z850 index region. Full field-level production requires adapting the supplied scripts’ archive loaders and configuring paths. The original production script also retrains the observation operator using external NCEP/NCAR R1 fields; reusing the packaged operator-space observations and observation-error variances instead requires an additional code adaptation. Modern verification and other full-pipeline analyses require additional external AGCM and reanalysis inputs, as described in REPRODUCE.md . The ten historical prior members are included, but the broader raw AGCM archive and most external reanalysis source fields are not. The manuscript and rendered figure files are not distributed in this package. CREAM-authored data, code, and documentation are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) license. summary: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), yet accurate FP4 quantization remains challenging. Practical formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 pair a 4-bit floating-point payload with block-wise or hierarchical scale codes, making accuracy highly sensitive to how each local distribution is scaled. Default maximum-absolute-value scaling preserves dynamic range, but can spend scarce FP4 levels on rarely occupied outlier regions and leave dense tensor values poorly resolved. Existing scale-search methods minimize local element-wise reconstruction error, optimizing tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity. We propose SoScale, a second-order weight scale-code search method for hierarchical FP4 quantization. SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective and couples this search with GPTQ-style error recovery, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs. Across Qwen3 models, SoScale consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4.
title: SoScale: Second-Order Scale Search for FP4 Quantization

summary: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.
title: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models

summary: We study $d$-dimensional quantum linear bandits with bounded rewards, where the learner selects an action and queries its quantum reward oracle or its inverse in each round. For general action sets, existing algorithms achieve regret $O(d^{3/2}\operatorname{polylog}(T))$ over $T$ rounds. Prior work established a lower bound of $Ω(d\log(1+T/d))$, leaving open whether the $d^{3/2}$ dependence in the upper bound is necessary. We resolve this question by proving a minimax lower bound of $Ω(d^{3/2}\log(1+T/d^{3/2}))$. To prove this result, we construct a family of hard instances in which the reward gap of each action is proportional to its squared distance from the optimal action. We establish a posterior Fisher information bound for adaptive quantum queries with quantum memory, relating the information acquired about the optimal direction to the regret incurred. Viewing each selected action as an estimate of the optimal direction, we use a matrix Cramér--Rao argument to derive a lower bound on expected regret. When the action set is fixed and has size $K$, we propose two phased elimination algorithms, Soft-G-Elim and QG-Elim. We adapt quantum phase estimation to construct SoftQME, a mean estimator with small bias and controlled tails. Soft-G-Elim estimates the mean reward of every surviving action from independent SoftQME outputs on the support of an experimental design. Controlling the bias and fluctuations of these estimates yields regret $O(d\log T\log(dT)\sqrt{\log(KT)})$, reducing the $\log(KT)\log\log(dT)$ factor in the previous regret bound to $\sqrt{\log(KT)}$. QG-Elim further reduces this factor to $\min\{\sqrt{\log(KT)},\sqrt d\}$.

summary: Survival in neonatal intensive care has improved faster than the developmental and psychological outcomes that follow it. Preterm infants show unstable autonomic regulation, and their parents report anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress far above population rates — two problems that are usually studied apart. This review asks whether care delivered by the parent acts on both at once. Searching Scopus from January 2020 to May 2026, we retrieved 160 records and included 90 studies, 52 of them randomised. Five intervention families were identified: skin-to-skin contact (28), parental psychoeducation (23), family-integrated care (21), parental voice and touch (16), and digital or telehealth support (2). Synthesis followed PRISMA 2020 and SWiM, with risk of bias assessed by RoB 2 and ROBINS-I and certainty by GRADE. Five trials (N = 494) supported a random-effects meta-analysis of parental distress: Hedges  g = −0.75 (95% CI, Hartung–Knapp, −1.32 to −0.19; p = 0.021; I² = 85.0%). The heterogeneity resolved to a single source — the one trial measuring depressive symptoms months after discharge; restricting to in-admission stress measurement gave g = −0.94 with I² = 0%. Effect-direction synthesis across the remaining 85 studies showed a gradient by proximity to the parent: parent–infant bonding 85.7% ( p = 0.003), infant autonomic regulation 77.8% ( p = 0.004), parental stress and PTSD 73.7% ( p = 0.013), falling to 56.3% for infant growth and 54.5% for length of stay. One trial of video-based home monitoring after cardiac surgery showed excess readmissions, retained as a comparator-favouring result rather than folded into “no difference”. The share of favourable results fell from 100% to 56% as design rigour increased (χ² = 10.91, p = 0.028). Four of 160 papers used any machine-learning method; none reported a clinical prediction model, and none linked neonatal risk stratification to structured family support.
title: GENEDIS 2026 – Paper 135 - Parent-Delivered Interventions and the Neonatal Regulatory Axis: A Systematic Reviw and Metaanalysis of Psychoeducation, Skin-to-Skin Contact and Family Integrated Care on Parental Mental Health and Infant Neurodevelopmental Outcomes

summary: Shifting populations toward diets that are simultaneously healthier and more environmentally sustainable is a central objective of food policy, yet self-report captures only a fraction of the rapid, partly non-conscious processes that govern food selection. This review synthesises neurophysiological evidence on those mechanisms, drawing on electroencephalography (EEG), eye-tracking and electrodermal activity (EDA/GSR). A structured Scopus search returned 350 records, screened in three stages to 30 eligible studies, grouped into three clusters of ten: food communication and labelling; choice environment and multisensory context; and consumer state and self-regulatory processes. A neurophysiological or attentional effect was detected in 27 of the 30 studies, and a downstream food outcome was assessed in 24. Among the 21 studies satisfying both conditions, 17 showed a corresponding behavioural or evaluative change and 4 showed attentional or affective capture without any change — the latter concentrated in manipulations competing against established preference, sensory appeal or habitual routine. Electrocortical indices (frontal alpha asymmetry, N2, P3, N400, LPP) tracked motivational relevance, valuation conflict and inhibitory control, while electrodermal indices tracked arousal that was dissociable from, and at times more predictive than, explicit evaluation. Sustainability framing was markedly under-represented relative to health framing (7 studies against 21), with a single study providing electrophysiological evidence on pro-environmental purchasing directly. Because the corpus invokes 15 distinct theoretical frames, none shared by more than six studies, the review proposes a three-stage integrative framework — attentional capture, affective arousal, and evaluative elaboration and control — with two documented failure gates and a state-and-trait modulation band. A pre-specified feasibility appraisal was conducted in place of a meta-analysis. Only 8 of 30 studies reported means, standard deviations and cell sizes jointly, 12 reported an extractable effect estimate, and 4 reported confidence intervals, with a median sample of approximately 32 participants. No outcome family combined sufficient study numbers with sufficient reporting, so a structured synthesis without meta-analysis is reported in accordance with the SWiM guideline, together with the reporting and harmonisation changes that would make quantitative synthesis achievable.

A pre-specified feasibility appraisal was conducted in place of a meta-analysis. Only 8 of 30 studies reported means, standard deviations and cell sizes jointly, 12 reported an extractable effect estimate, and 4 reported confidence intervals, with a median sample of approximately 32 participants. No outcome family combined sufficient study numbers with sufficient reporting, so a structured synthesis without meta-analysis is reported in accordance with the SWiM guideline, together with the reporting and harmonisation changes that would make quantitative synthesis achievable.

summary: The manuscript gives a proposed learning algorithm for an unknown polynomially sparse Pauli Hamiltonian of operator norm at most one, using only forward evolution queries whose durations are all at least a fixed positive constant T. It obtains maximum coefficient error epsilon with constant success probability and total evolution time polynomial in the qubit number and sparsity, divided by epsilon, up to logarithmic factors. Circuit and classical processing costs are polynomial; constants may depend on T. The construction uses a two-time residual inverse and does not assume controlled access to, or the inverse of, the unknown evolution. This deposit preserves the website manuscript, version 1.0, dated 1 October 2026, by Yuxuan Zhang. It is a complete proof candidate with internal review and supporting checks; independent expert verification and exhaustive priority confirmation remain outstanding. Website and supporting material: https://yuxuanzhang1995.github.io/agentic-research/fixed-duration-hamiltonian-learning/ QIQC original: https://qiqc-op.com/problem/op_30954594cf01ebb3/
title: Heisenberg-scaling sparse Hamiltonian learning with a fixed minimum query duration

summary: Transect-level shoreline change rates (Theil–Sen, tide-corrected with EOT20, tan β = 0.1) for 12,787 sandy open-coast transects (2 km spacing) in Indonesia, 2013 to 31 October 2026, from Landsat 8/9 Collection 2 Level 2 imagery in Google Earth Engine. Includes sand-classifier probabilities for 36,765 candidate transects, training labels (first-pass, authors’ Sentinel-2 consensus, high-resolution), cross-validation and robustness diagnostics, the earlier 2013–2025 baseline for comparison, and processing scripts. Intended for screening, not site design: roughly one third of transects classed sandy are expected to be false positives, labels come from the authors, and rates are subject to a ±100 m search window and uniform beach slope. Accompanies a manuscript submitted to Civil Engineering Journal.
title: Shoreline change rates along sandy coasts of the Indonesian archipelago, Landsat 8/9, 2013–31 October 2026 (transect-level dataset and code)

summary: Coded dataset, document manifest and analysis code behind every figure, table and statistical test reported in the paper. Thirty-six Malaysian listed organizations in three strata of regulatory attention are coded on four governance dimensions — fairness, transparency, accountability and privacy — giving 144 organization-dimension cells. Each cell takes the highest level found anywhere in that organization’s corpus: 0 no AI-specific disclosure on that dimension, 1 an artifact is stated to exist, 2 an activity is described as performed, 3 a retrievable instance is reported. Every cell carries the basis note recording the passage and page it rests on. Contents. 18 CSV files, including the coding of record, four second-coder files from the reliability work and the manifest of all 79 source documents. 17 Python analysis scripts requiring no third-party packages except matplotlib for the figures. 37 working notes from coding and adjudication, and the sealed passage sets used for the second, independent application of the codebook. Reproduction. README.md lists the command that regenerates each reported result, including the four inter-coder comparisons and the four alternative readings of the coding. Not included. The 79 source documents are the copyright of the organizations that published them and are not redistributed. All are public. corpus.csv and Appendix B of the paper list every one with its page count, so the corpus can be reconstructed independently from the issuers’ own websites and from Bursa Malaysia. The second application of the coding protocol reported in Section 4 of the paper was carried out by a language model agent supplied with the codebook and the passage set, not by a trained human coder. The reported agreement figures therefore test whether the codebook can be followed consistently rather than inter-rater reliability in the usual sense.
title: Replication data and code for "Policy Without Evidence: A Three-Level Measure of Artificial Intelligence Governance Disclosure by Malaysian Boards"

summary: Therapeutic exercise is recommended for people with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), yet it remains unclear whether adding structured cognitive training to an exercise programme already incorporating dual-task activities provides additional benefit beyond the physical programme itself. This protocol describes a single-blind, three-arm randomised controlled trial of a multicomponent motor–motor dual-task exercise programme for people with MCI (MExeProMCI), with and without a superimposed structured cognitive-training programme. Fortyfive community-dwelling adults over 50 years with amnestic MCI (Montreal Cognitive Assessment ≥20) are allocated (1:1:1) to MExeProMCI-Cog, the dualtask exercise programme plus structured cognitive training; to MExeProMCI, the same programme without additional cognitive training; or to a control group receiving an educational leaflet. The primary outcome is dynamic balance, assessed with the mini-Balance Evaluation Systems Test (mini-BESTest). Secondary outcomes include functional gait, three-dimensional gait analysis during single- and dual-task walking and obstacle crossing, cognition, executive function, physical performance, fear of falling, mood, neuropsychiatric symptoms and adherence. Assessors are blinded and the primary analysis is an analysis of covariance adjusted for baseline scores on an intention-to-treat basis. Comparing the two active arms will determine whether structured cognitive training adds benefit beyond the exercise programme alone. The trial is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07334392).
title: Structured Cognitive Training Added to the Multicomponent Exercise Programme in Amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment: Protocol for a Single-Blind, Three-Arm Randomised Controlled Trial

summary: Frozen pre-registration of a study that compares smoke-dependent exit choice in pyFDS-Evac (JuPedSim coupled with FDS 6.10.1) with survivor exit-use data from The Station Nightclub fire (Fahy et al. 2011, Table 2). It was frozen before the first production FDS fire run. This archive is the source tree of the pyFDS-Evac repository at tag station-prereg-v1 (commit aaeda1f3). The directory assets/station_prereg/ contains: preregistration.md: targets, registered criteria and bands, run design, arms and sensitivities, fire inputs, outputs already seen, failure policy, and changes from the study plan; freeze_record.md: software versions, build, run and scoring commands for every arm, and seeds; fds/: the six FDS input decks (0.2 m central, low and high yields, ±15 s HRR shift; 0.1 m grid check), their generator, and the HRR curve digitised from NIST NCSTAR 2 Fig. 5-42; SHA256SUMS: checksums of these files, the scenario configs, the scoring script and uv.lock. The study is a comparison with survivor exit-use data, not a validation and not a forensic reconstruction. Any registered criterion that fails will be reported as a disclosed failure.
title: Pre-registration of the Station Nightclub coupled fire–evacuation study with pyFDS-Evac (station-prereg-v1)

summary: Observed Palworld stat values support a binary32 passive percent round trip, food-rate corrections, additive partner bonuses and an inclusive 30% hunger threshold, with HP unaffected by hunger. This dataset accompanies Lore Armory's v2.0 technical note for build 25246127 and contains 2,400 checked stat values across worlds A–K, distinguishing the later K2 pass and repeated party or fullness states. All have numerical predictions and match; four previously unavailable H predictions are now retrospective calculations from recovered case inputs. The observation basis distinguishes 1,834 individual numerical readbacks from 566 outcomes explicitly confirmed equal to named predictions for completed sets. The CSV records each available case label, species, level, inputs, prediction, observation and comparison status, and preserves original frozen predictions where available so that later corrections cannot be mistaken for prior confirmation. Six public mathematical copies of F–K prediction sheets retain selected and rival values, with the original commitment list, a separate checksum manifest for the public copies, and the superseded, unchecked J v1 status. The original and public-copy hashes refer to different bytes. The README supplies a hand calculation, column definitions, exact count filters, observation provenance and open questions. The rows reproduce every empirical headline count in the note; overlapping scoring subsets are explicitly marked. The package does not imply confirmation of every partner star level, food-plus-hunger evaluation order or game build.
title: Palworld Pal stat verification: observations and frozen predictions (v2.0.1)

summary: Multimodal depression screening estimates risk from speech, visual behavior and language. Current methods mainly predict labels, with limited evidence of departures from a non-depressed reference. Recording-level supervision also leaves fine-grained emotional dynamics unannotated. Motivated by emotional inertia, the persistence of affect, InertiaMPDD learns healthy next-state patterns using a world-model-inspired latent predictor. Using pretrained multimodal representations, it predicts from observed history and context. Reference deviation, residual decay rate and a Jacobian spectral descriptor form reference-derived emotional dynamics descriptors, evaluated as candidate proxy biomarkers for standalone screening and personalized decision correction. Across five cohorts from four datasets, fusion reaches 98.41% F1 on D-Vlog and 84.98% on LMVD. Standalone descriptors outperform fixed additive fusion on MPDD but discriminate weakly on AVEC2014. These findings distinguish reference informativeness from fusion benefit and reveal context-dependent utility.
title: InertiaMPDD: Multimodal Personalized Depression Detection via Emotional Inertia-Inspired Dynamics Modeling

summary: This repository provides the Python implementations, numerical datasets, verification scripts, and supporting computational results associated with the manuscript “Finite-Amplitude Tipping in Tumor Escape Organized by Hypoxia–Immune–Matrix Feedback” . The study investigates nonlinear tumor–immune dynamics using a six-state mechanistic model coupling immunogenic and immune-escape tumor phenotypes, innate and adaptive immune responses, oxygen availability, and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Particular attention is given to finite-amplitude oscillations arising through a subcritical Hopf bifurcation and a limit point of cycles (LPC), resulting in equilibrium–cycle bistability and perturbation-dependent transitions. Version 2 (v2) preserves the original numerical archive and extends the computational reproducibility materials with additional analyses and verification procedures developed during manuscript revision. The principal additions include: Generalized-Hopf analysis and investigation of reversible phenotype conversion. Ablation-specific Hopf and LPC calculations to assess the contributions of hypoxia-mediated conversion and immune-pressure feedback. Directional basin-threshold calculations and extended numerical integrations. Expanded parameter-sensitivity and robustness analyses. Additional shooting-based and adaptive-collocation verification of periodic solutions. Floquet stability screening of 252 periodic orbits, including a targeted assessment of potential period-doubling behavior. Updated bifurcation figures, numerical results, parameter provenance documentation, and reproducibility instructions.
title: Finite-Amplitude Tipping in Tumor Escape: Numerical Simulation Data, Bifurcation Analysis, and Computational Reproducibility

summary: What information about environmental memory must a quantum controller retain to guarantee a specified computational output? This preprint formulates that question in terms of task-sufficient process representations, intervention-valid predictions, stochastic clock laws, and explicit resource accounting. The central requirement is to preserve the outcomes and costs of the permitted decisions, with a stated accuracy contract and a finite-sample certificate. The paper connects two complementary lines of analysis. An operational construction studies Gaussian dephasing and controlled qubit tasks. A separate stochastic-clock analysis studies direct and inverse time changes, fractional relaxation, and the information that temporal coarse graining must transport. These constructions address related modelling questions but are not identified as a single microscopic noise model. The main elements are: Identical uncontrolled channels, different controlled responses. A continuum of Gaussian phase processes has the same uncontrolled coherence at every time and zero Breuer-Laine-Piilo backflow, yet different spin-echo responses. The construction shows why an uncontrolled channel family alone can fail to determine an intervention-dependent control decision. Task-sufficient equivalence and resource contracts. The manuscript defines a contract functional collecting accepted-output moments, acceptance probabilities, and physical costs over a declared policy family. Its finite linear task quotient identifies distinctions relevant to those predictions. Approximate sufficiency is accompanied by stability bounds that expose the sensitivity of conditional guarantees to low acceptance probabilities and small feasibility margins. Simultaneous finite-policy certification. Conservative confidence bounds certify conditional task bias and expected cost per accepted outcome after selection among a fixed, finite set of candidate policies. The assumptions include independent reset attempts, bounded observations and costs, and a trusted ideal reference. Failure to certify a candidate is explicitly distinguished from proof that no feasible physical policy exists. An explicit coarse-graining framework for stochastic clocks. The proposed decorated phase space records the process, permitted policy family, observable set, and clock law. The clock component transports stable laws under their natural scaling and relates domains of attraction to regular variation of waiting-time tails. Within the stated two-parameter clock-and-coupling family, the relaxation-rate direction scales with eigenvalue c^alpha. These clock results are placed in the established probabilistic renormalization literature; they do not establish hyperbolicity or convergence for the full decorated operator. A reset-sensitive fractional-relaxation calculation. Direct subordination of a quantum dynamical semigroup is distinguished from inverse-stable time change. For the latter, the paper compares uninterrupted evolution with independent renewal of the hidden clock and relevant environment. At half order and dimensionless rate one, the exact erfcx representation gives the short-time defect Delta(h) ~ 0.660989212585294 sqrt(h). The difference concerns the declared reset protocols, rather than a general assertion that every physical gate resets its environment. The reported classical benchmark uses ten candidate policies with explicit pulse depolarisation and separate X- and Z-expectation contracts. At the quasistatic endpoint, midpoint echo increases average identity-gate fidelity from 0.789293 to 0.990050. The fidelity crossover near r = 0.0467883 is distinct from the stricter X-task feasibility threshold r >= 0.9688074. For the selected Z-task input, dephasing is harmless and unnecessary echo pulses reduce the expectation. Conventional calibrated echo matches the best tested control performance; calibration, sampling, rejected attempts, and amortisation remain part of the resource account. Two q

summary: RadVeil removes identifiable facial and auricular (ear) surfaces from NIfTI head MRI and CT. It localizes the face the way an attacker would -- rendering the volume as a portrait and running a 2D face detector -- and accepts an anonymization only when re-detection on the output fails. Ears are located from surface evidence (protrusion detection against a scalp baseline) rather than fixed anatomical offsets. Every voxel outside the exported mask is preserved bit-exact, with datatype, scaling and header intact.
title: RadVeil: CPU-only face and ear anonymization for volumetric head imaging

summary: This report and reproducibility package examine how a specified receiver determines which distinctions in a supplied nested quantum state become accessible in its measurement records. Two nonorthogonal states with unequal 70/30 population weights and opposite coherence have identical reduced states on every nonempty proper subset of their encoded registers. Measurements confined to those subsets cannot distinguish the candidates. Local equatorial measurements followed by comparison of their records reveal a joint parity contrast, whose accessibility depends on the receiver phase. For the worked two-register example, equal-prior single-trial discrimination succeeds with probability 95.83% under ideal retention and 79.33% with independent 80% retention at each receiver. These probabilities include incomplete records. Blind receiver settings and complete dephasing provide distinct zero-contrast controls. The report also establishes reconstruction from three real quantities within a known two-dimensional encoded subspace. A support-leakage counterexample demonstrates why this reconstruction does not extend to unrestricted states. All sixteen numerical check families pass, including 5,130 proper-subset comparisons. A verification run reproduces the archived scientific results exactly. The package includes the report, executable code, fixed configuration, numerical results, probability tables, figures, equation sources, report builder and checksums. This is an analytic and computational benchmark within declared quantum states and measurement models. It provides a bounded example of receiver-dependent information access and candidate-state identification; it does not constitute experimental validation or derive a physical mechanism of nesting.
title: Receiver Distinguishability of Nested States

Two nonorthogonal states with unequal 70/30 population weights and opposite coherence have identical reduced states on every nonempty proper subset of their encoded registers. summary: GPU-native Julia framework for CT and photon-counting CT simulation, reconstruction, and quantitative spectral imaging. Provides distance-driven forward projection (with Siddon ray tracing as an alternative), polychromatic Beer-Lambert physics with vendor-realistic detector response (MC-derived LUTs for GE Gemstone scintillator and Siemens NAEOTOM Alpha CdTe), FDK, helical WFBP and hybrid iterative reconstruction, sinogram and image-domain beam-hardening correction, projection-domain dual-kVp and PCCT material decomposition (K-channel profile likelihood, Cong 2022), spectral denoising, and virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI + Grant 2014 Mono+) — all dispatching transparently across CPU, Metal, CUDA, and ROCm via AcceleratedKernels.jl.
title: BasisSimulator.jl: Open-source polychromatic CT simulation with a GPU-portable reconstruction stack

summary: A law $F$ with mean $\mu$ is $n$-completely mixable if there are $n$ random variables with law $F$ whose sum is almost surely $n\mu$. Wang proved that such a law satisfies a family of inequalities between the norms of the positive and negative parts of $X-t$ and $X-s$, where $X\sim F$ and $s=(n\mu-t)/(n-1)$, for every threshold $t$ and every law-determined norm, and asked when these inequalities are also sufficient (Open Problem 4 in his 2015 survey). We show that for bounded $F$ the whole family is equivalent to the single convex-order condition $X-\mu\cx-(n-1)(X-\mu)$, and that the same holds for integrable $F$ if the norms are required to have the Fatou property. The inequalities do not imply $n$-complete mixability: for $n=3$ the analytic density $\frac1{10}+\frac{27}{10}(2x-1)^2$ on $[0,1]$ satisfies all of them and is not $3$-completely mixable, and for $n=3$ and $n=4$ there are counterexamples with densities bounded away from zero on $[0,1]$ and with $C^\infty$ densities, the one for $n=4$ not symmetric. A Bernoulli$(p)$ law satisfies the inequalities exactly when $1/n\le p\le1-1/n$, while it is $n$-completely mixable exactly when $np$ is an integer. For $n=2$ the inequalities are equivalent to symmetry, hence to $2$-complete mixability, for every integrable law.
title: Law-determined norm inequalities do not imply complete mixability

summary: Woody Crown Hydraulic Network (WCHN): mathematical revisions, corrected datasets, and reproducible computational resources This repository provides an integrated historical, empirical, and computational resource for the Woody Crown Hydraulic Network (WCHN) framework. It brings together the foundational development of the model, original and corrected crown-network records, recalculated WCHN properties, ecological comparisons, principal component analyses (PCAs), editable network drawings, and computational tools for reconstructing and analyzing woody crown networks. The deposit is an independent scientific resource, not tied to any particular journal or manuscript. HISTORICAL FOUNDATION Four publications document the development of the WCHN framework: Souza et al. (2011): initial network analyses of Cerrado tree crowns. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11258-010-9797-7 Prado et al. (2020): formalization of network decomposition, topology, and the four original properties. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2020.110318 Prado and Trovão (2023): expansion to eight properties and comparative analyses of Caatinga and Cerrado networks. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2023.110345 Prado (2024): stochastic node-addition networks and size-matched comparisons. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40626-024-00340-5 These references enable users to trace the original definitions, subsequent revisions, and development of the framework. INDEPENDENT MATHEMATICAL REFERENCE The definitions, revised equations, algebraic identities, mathematical properties, conditions of definition, and theoretical implications of the WCHN framework are now documented in a separate, independently published and versioned Zenodo record: Prado (2026). Algebraic Relationships and Mathematical Properties of the Woody Crown Hydraulic Network (WCHN). Version 1.0.0. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24181915 This mathematical reference includes the revised definitions of symmetry (SYM), complexity (COM), and topological vulnerability (VUL); exact algebraic relationships among WCHN properties; network-size dependence; and mathematical and numerical checks. In particular, revised VUL is equivalent to normalized mean node depth in a rooted tree. The near-reciprocity observed between navigability (NAV) and VUL is an empirical relationship, not an additional algebraic identity or evidence of physiological equivalence. The mathematical document was included in an earlier version of the present dataset deposit. Beginning with the current version, it is maintained exclusively in its independent Zenodo record. Earlier published versions retain their original archived files for historical traceability. EMPIRICAL DATASETS AND ECOLOGICAL REANALYSES The deposit contains the original Cerrado and Caatinga source spreadsheets, recalculated WCHN properties, ecological comparisons, reduced PCAs, and exploratory network-size-adjusted analyses. The complete field collection comprises 99 WCHNs: 75 from Cerrado and 24 from Caatinga. Recalculated tables incorporate the revised SYM, COM, and VUL definitions. The reduced PCAs use NAV, VUL, LAT, BAS, and PTP, with 24 Caatinga networks and 74 complete Cerrado networks. Previously deposited PCA and partial-correlation results are preserved without numerical recalculation in this update. Their interpretation should account for network-size dependence, shared topological information, and the revised mathematical meaning of VUL. The accompanying README_Size_Adjusted_PCA_v2.md documents the methods, results, assumptions, and limitations of the size-adjusted analyses. CORRECTED CERRADO NETWORKS AND REPRODUCIBLE TOOLKIT The deposit includes a workbook documenting corrections to 20 previously sampled Cerrado WCHNs. These are corrected records of existing observations, not additional independent networks. Six networks were reconstructed manually, including S. polyphyllum 1 as the manual feasibility pilot.
