A LETTER FROM THE RESEARCH GENERATION A successful assisted action is an astonishingly incomplete explanation. The hand may rise because a person acts, because a robot lifts, because an elastic interface returns stored energy, or because the observer failed to record a missing contact force. When support has been removed, the original appearance of success can disappear without contradiction: the two tests were measuring different capacities. This notebook begins by giving that distinction the dignity of a research problem rather than quietly merging it into a single performance score. The integrated F086-F090 family proposes five mechanisms. First, assistance must be minimized under safety and accuracy constraints. Next, an independent force audit must distinguish who performed the work. Then withdrawal timing becomes an intervention, not an inconvenience. A fourth study asks whether observed movement is actively generated or passively imposed. Finally, a blinded device-off and unfamiliar-task probe asks what remains without the apparatus. All these studies can be falsified on an inert mechanical-hand bench or an offline synthetic replay platform. They do not constitute a clinical evaluation. Our five-stage parallel spacetime reasoning is an intellectual strategy: lock the origin of the question, formalize candidate relations, allow a rival causal world, discover limits through safe bounded stress, and transfer the contradiction to a future laboratory. summary: This preprint evaluates a reversible sample mapping that embeds 8-bit RGB values in the central half of a 9-bit sRGB code space before lossy JPEG XL encoding. The stored file includes a five-byte header that identifies the inverse mapping. The evaluation covers 41 previously unused CLIC Professional and DIV2K validation images at their original resolutions. Under common RGB PSNR and MS-SSIM floors and a single-thread encoding cap of 0.82 seconds per megapixel, the centered mapping reduced aggregate file size by 6.71% relative to direct JPEG XL at effort 6 (95% bootstrap interval: 3.85% to 9.86%). The centered files were 3.94% larger in aggregate than the tested AVIF files. Same-depth and transfer-function controls, together with libjxl coding counters, examine how the input representation affects the result.
title: Centered Sample-Range Remapping at JPEG XL Effort 6

STROKE MOTOR INTENTION AND BRAIN-COMPUTER RESEARCH F081-F085 | SCIENTIFIC TECHNICAL NOTEBOOK | RESEARCH WORKING EDITION Prospective | Nonclinical | Falsifiable | Reproducible | Unbuilt Research Concepts 33 x STARLI OPENING ESSAY | THE AUTHORITY A MODEL DOES NOT HAVE A brain-computer interface is tempting to describe as a bridge between thought and action. But the bridge is only useful when we know what went into the decoder. An electrode voltage is a mixture of cortical, muscle, eye, reference and environmental processes. A task label may record what was instructed rather than what was imagined. A camera can record what moved but not what a person intended. This family treats those distinctions as independent scientific objects, not inconvenient details. The five flagship questions are coupled without being identical. F081 asks whether EEG adds information about spontaneous motor intention after cue clocks and residual muscle activity are accounted for. F082 distinguishes imagery, attempted movement and overt displacement with independent electromyographic and visual witnesses. F083 measures what remains stable across recording days. F084 resists the temptation to hide weak-signal and rare-class strata in a pooled score. F085 observes the safety consequences of false intention triggers during long periods of silence. The minimal platform is an anonymous, synthetic EEG-EMG-EOG task replayer with inert video coordinates, frozen event timestamps and a virtual command queue. The test generator can provide a hidden latent state to evaluate conditional identification. The model never sees that latent state during inference; it must work from the channels and timing evidence available at the specified decision moment. This is a deliberate computational thought experiment and nonclinical engineering proposal, not a physical experiment on stroke survivors. Several rival accounts deserve equal space. Cue onset may encode movement class because the task schedule is regular. Eye motion may precede an instruction. EMG can influence scalp electrodes before obvious displacement occurs. A test-day montage can reveal which session generated a signal. A preprocessing transform can learn the distribution or labels of the held-out partition. A fair protocol separates these shortcuts from useful cortical information with interventions that are physically or informationally interpretable. The real methodological enemy is the persuasive but under-identified success. A model can predict a motor class accurately without identifying voluntary intent. A classifier can distinguish imagery from actual movement using residual muscle activity, not imagination. A transfer algorithm can report stable day-to-day performance after silently adapting on test-day labels. A strong subgroup average can hide dangerous errors among weak signals. Even a correctly predicted category cannot justify a virtual or physical action without authorization and a safety envelope. Prediction and clinical recovery are separate propositions. The current manuscript does not study human participants, deliver rehabilitative interventions or report therapeutic efficacy. Device-driven motion is not device-off recovery. A physical, clinically authorized program would need separate ethical review, independent recruitment, preregistered outcomes and direct functional observation. Our synthetic graphs, however detailed, cannot stand in for that evidence. The most useful classical competitors should not be artificially weak. Cue-only prediction tests whether the experiment provided all the information needed. CSP-LDA, regularized logistic models, Riemannian covariance methods and explicit EMG-video rules can challenge a complex learner with equal data access. Calibration, preprocessing, sensor count, trial duration and temporal alignment all form part of cost. A negative finding can reveal the true measurement limit more effectively than an elaborate but unearned claim of superiority. A scientific three-dimensional plate is a way to expose a functional relationship, not to ornament it. Each surface in the PDF is computed from a documented analytic rule on an exact numeric grid. The outputs are synthetic normalized proxies. The embedded JSON and Python program permit independent recomputation of all forty-two plates. The table of physical units explains what a real EEG, EMG, video or queue experiment would have to measure before the candidate relation could be considered more than a hypothesis. The five-stage parallel spacetime method provides a language for organizing scientific alternatives. Origin questions define the unknown, formal models specify the proposed mechanism, counterfactual branches give rivals room to win, bounded extreme scenarios locate failure, and successor reconstruction transfers the case to a new laboratory. It is a method of intellectual branching. It does not assert that parallel universes were used to calculate a result. Research Gates are deliberately invitations rather than final proofs. In the first set, each door asks how a particular motor-intention ambiguity began. The next set gives conventional signal processing the right to defeat the proposed mechanism. The third constructs unfamiliar but bounded artifact worlds. The fourth gives an independent laboratory the raw history needed to rebuild a result. The final set asks what a technically advanced successor might overturn. Their varying tones should not be mistaken for different measured data; these are different arguments about possible experiments. The thirty-three Phoenix concepts are instruments that do not yet exist in verified form. Some would preserve cue-blind intention witnesses, some audit the cost of daily calibration, and others observe false triggers or the latency of a safety stop in an inert queue. Each prototype has a measurable target and a defined failure. None is authorized as a clinical device. The scientific ambition is to leave an implementable and criticizable question, not to make a claim about unbuilt hardware. For additional methodological context, TRIPOD+AI (DOI 10.1136/bmj-2023-078378) specifies transparent reporting for prediction-model studies. A review of cross-variability decoding of motor-imagery EEG (PubMed 42775222) identifies major challenges in subject/session variability and nonstationarity. These sources motivate reporting discipline and uncertainty; they do not certify our integrated candidate family or any claimed treatment effect. A living scientific manuscript need not be immutable. If future methods show that all five present hypotheses were based on crude modeling, that correction would be welcome. What should survive is the habit of showing independent clocks, an ordinary rival, a missing signal, a false command and an unambiguous stop. The knowledge of how to ask the question is one part of what we can leave to a future investigator. THE FIVE DISTINCT FLAGSHIP CONTRACTS F081 | Post-Stroke Motor Intention EEG Decoding at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: identify preparatory cortical signal beyond cue clocks and residual muscle activity in an offline intention replay. Declared primary observables: cue-controlled balanced accuracy [1], conditional information [bit], false triggers [events/h]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that a decoder memorizes the cue time, recording day or ocular artifact instead of voluntary intention. The concealed discriminating test should blindly permute cue timing while maintaining the source EEG event structure. Instrumental evidence: source-separated synthetic EEG [microvolts], EMG [mV], EOG [microvolts], cue clocks [ms], free-choice intention events and versioned trial IDs. A strong baseline is cue-only timing predictor, regularized logistic EEG classifier, Riemannian covariance baseline and CSP-LDA trained only within sealed source folds. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F082 | Distinguishing Motor Imagery from Actual Movement After Stroke at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: disentangle motor imagery, attempted movement, residual EMG and camera-observed motion under masked timing. Declared primary observables: imagery-movement confusion [1], residual EMG amplitude [mV], intention lead [ms]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that subthreshold muscle contractions or eye movements masquerade as imagery-dependent EEG features. The concealed discriminating test should withhold the EMG-video agreement channel and test synthetic no-movement imagery trials. Instrumental evidence: inert EEG [microvolts], bilateral EMG [mV], synchronized video position [mm], intended task classes and blinded motion adjudication. A strong baseline is video-EMG heuristic with blinded thresholds, temporal-kernel baseline, CSP-LDA and balanced multi-modal classifier without future labels. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F083 | Cross-Day Signal Stability of Stroke Brain-Computer Interfaces at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: test whether frozen motor-intention decoders remain calibrated across independently replayed electrode days. Declared primary observables: cross-day balanced accuracy [1], ECE [1], drift alarm time [s]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that a short-session score hides montage shifts, fatigue and re-calibration leakage. The concealed discriminating test should swap a held-out electrode montage and sleep-fatigue profile without recalibrating on the test day. Instrumental evidence: multiday EEG [microvolts], contact/montage manifests, synthetic sleep-fatigue shifts, acquisition timestamps [ms] and frozen calibration tokens. A strong baseline is session-independent logistic model, Riemannian alignment, frozen calibration and correctly budgeted classical domain adaptation. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F084 | Individual Variability in Post-Stroke Motor Intention Decoding at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: separate actual subject-specific latent signal differences from subgroup prevalence and unequal annotation reliability. Declared primary observables: worst-stratum sensitivity [1], subgroup ECE [1], missing-label fraction [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that pooled accuracy hides poor performance under low signal-to-noise or severe synthetic impairment. The concealed discriminating test should hold out an entire synthetic severity stratum with matched cue and artifact distributions. Instrumental evidence: synthetic signal-to-noise strata [dB], missing label indicators, subject-day lineage IDs, group size [count] and held-out subgroup reports. A strong baseline is hierarchical calibration, subgroup-stratified logistic classifier, mixed-effects model and transparent missing-label sensitivity bounds. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F085 | Safety Against False Intention Triggers in Stroke BCIs at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: suppress mistaken intention-triggered commands using calibrated abstention, authorization and inert safe-stop simulation. Declared primary observables: false activations [events/h], refusal delay [ms], risk-coverage AUC [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that rare false positives disappear in averaged accuracy and queueing masks stop latency. The concealed discriminating test should inject a novel false-positive EEG artifact while tracking end-to-end inactive command and veto logs. Instrumental evidence: long no-intention segments [h], inert dispatch queue logs [ms], artifact identities, policy tokens, refusal decisions and error-event records. A strong baseline is fixed threshold and debounce rules, calibrated selective classifier, independent artifact sentinel and fail-closed policy interlock. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment.

F082 | Distinguishing Motor Imagery from Actual Movement After Stroke at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: disentangle motor imagery, attempted movement, residual EMG and camera-observed motion under masked timing. F085 | Safety Against False Intention Triggers in Stroke BCIs at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: suppress mistaken intention-triggered commands using calibrated abstention, authorization and inert safe-stop simulation. Declared primary observables: false activations [events/h], refusal delay [ms], risk-coverage AUC [1]. summary: We formulate a finite-core vorton representation of three-dimensional incompressible Navier– Stokes flow. Smooth divergence-free vorticity fields are represented by finite-core filamentary modes and studied in the limit of decreasing core scale. The singular vorton configuration is obtained strictly as a distributional concentration limit rather than imposed a priori as a singular solution. We prove dynamical equivalence by mapping the infinite-dimensional Navier–Stokes partial differential equations exactly onto the finite-dimensional ordinary differential equations of the discrete vorton ensemble. The passage through the nonlinear convective term is established via Mosco-type energy convergence and Aubin–Lions–Simon compactness. Topological reconnection supplies a microscopic writhe-to-twist transfer to regularize the ultraviolet limit, while a Fredholm boundary reconstruction controls wall interactions via weakly singular integral operators. The resulting framework proves that the continuum flow collapses onto an irreducible, compact geometric attractor, reducing global regularity to a uniform bound on vorticity and satisfying the Beale–Kato–Majda (BKM) criterion for global continuation.
title: RIGOROUS CONVERGENCE OF 3D NAVIER–STOKES TO A VORTON ATTRACTOR

No completed clinical experiment or quantum hardware advantage is asserted. 33 x STARLI | White Rainbow Era THE SECOND SCIENTIFIC VOICE: WHY THE DIGITAL TWIN MUST BE ALLOWED TO FAIL One reason digital twins feel persuasive is that they move. The screen appears to contain the limb, the muscles and the sensor history at once. Yet a moving virtual joint is not a second nervous system; it is a set of equations constrained by selected observations. The appearance of continuity may hide a fundamentally nonidentifiable physiological parameter, an electrode that shifted between sessions, or a modeling assumption that the subject never shared. This scientific notebook begins with that discomfort rather than with the promise of perfect prediction. It follows the difference between computing an answer and learning which hidden mechanism actually produced an observed record. The five flagships cannot be reduced to one accuracy score. F071 asks what can be inferred from movement when different latent parameters yield the same trajectory. F072 asks whether the observation itself has been calibrated, including cross-talk, electrode position and muscle force. F073 shifts the inquiry to a 4D microactuation interface where magnetic torque, heating, elastic deformation and microfluidics can interact. F074 asks whether uncertainty estimates retain their stated coverage on unseen conditions. F075 asks what remains when an independent laboratory runs the pipeline and times every stage. One book couples the five, but each must retain its own grounds for being wrong. Our shared minimum platform is a synthetic musculoskeletal model and offline, traceable validation sandbox. Physiological terms and metrics provide hypotheses for experiments; none of the plotted values represents a measurement from a stroke patient. A reproducible numerical curve does not establish that an implanted microrobot has functioned, that BCI intent has been decoded, or that unaided motor recovery has occurred. Those questions need their own governance and evidence. This work proposes methods to investigate them responsibly without transferring an unsupported prediction into an autonomous patient-facing command. The phrase five-stage parallel spacetime reasoning means intellectual plurality. In the first stage we identify the physical origin; in the second we derive a candidate model; in the third we let an ordinary competing explanation inhabit a serious counterfactual world; in the fourth we stress the limits of the claimed mechanism; and in the fifth we converge only on evidence another group can reconstruct. These are not literal alternate universes. They are repeated acts of taking a preferred hypothesis seriously enough to ask where it would fail. The creative process is valuable when it makes the experiment more discriminating, not when it generates more pages. Quantum computation enters these questions as a candidate technology, not a talisman. A variational or quantum-inspired optimizer still needs observations loaded, a parameterization chosen, an objective checked and a result validated. A well-tuned classical approach can be extraordinarily capable for systems of these sizes and tolerances. Credible comparisons must include the costs of encoding, queueing, runs, preprocessing and failed experiments. A lower intermediate objective is not necessarily a smaller predictive error, a more calibrated interval or a faster end-to-end workflow. The ordinary model is allowed to win. An inverse model can fit exceptionally well precisely because its parameterization is too flexible. Two latent settings may compensate for one another, producing an apparently narrow observed error while leaving the physiological cause unresolved. The correct response is to design a new excitation or independent witness, not simply search longer for a preferred optimum. Similarly, a confidence band may be over-wide and still exhibit nominal coverage. F074 makes both coverage and width observable, conditioned on shifts that the original model did not see. These examples are not exceptions to the value of mathematical models; they reveal why careful models are valuable. Published reviews and perspectives give context without validating this family's original integration. Predictive musculoskeletal simulation has a substantial classical methodology, with OpenSim and related tools documented in DOI 10.1186/s12984-025-01686-w. Digital-twin verification and uncertainty remain methodological challenges discussed in DOI 10.1038/s41746-025-01447-y. A scoping review of stroke rehabilitation twins appears at DOI 10.1080/10749357.2025.2584031. Fair quantum-optimization benchmarking has been developed in DOI 10.1038/s43588-026-00991-1. These works are backgrounds and competitors, not proof of advantage or recovery in the synthetic research family proposed here. Every scientific argument in this notebook is intended to leave a door. An investigator should know which parameter was not identified, which electrode drift changed the data, which finite-element assumption failed, which confidence interval missed, and which ordinary solver won. If a future scientist finds our equation obsolete, that is no betrayal. The success of a living research civilization is that it leaves behind enough units, code, counterfactuals and humility to be improved. A manuscript ends responsibly when its remaining uncertainties have become transferable experiments. summary: Routing-driven timely data collection in Underwater Acoustic Sensor Networks (UASNs) is crucial for marine environmental monitoring, disaster warning, and underwater resource exploration, etc. However, harsh underwater conditions, including high delays, limited bandwidth, and dynamic topologies, make efficient routing decisions challenging in UASNs. In this paper, we propose a smart interrupted routing scheme for UASNs to address dynamic underwater challenges. We first model underwater noise influences from real underwater routing features, e.g., turbulence and storms. We then propose a Software-Defined Networking (SDN)-based Interrupted Software-defined UASNs Reinforcement Learning (ISURL) framework, which ensures adaptive routing through dynamical failure handling (e.g., energy depletion of sensor nodes or link instability) and real-time interrupted recovery. Based on ISURL, we propose the MA-MAPPO algorithm, integrating multi-head attention mask mechanism with MAPPO to filter out infeasible actions and streamline training. Furthermore, to support interrupted data routing in UASNs, we introduce MA-MAPPO\_i, MA-MAPPO with interrupted policy, to enable smart interrupted routing decisions in UASNs. The evaluations demonstrate that our proposed routing scheme achieves exact underwater data routing decisions with faster convergence speed and lower routing delays than existing approaches.
title: Smart Interrupted Routing Based on Multi-head Attention Mask Mechanism-Driven MARL in Software-defined UASNs

It is not evidence that the model has identified a causal neural mechanism. It is not permission to issue a physical command. It is not a clinical outcome. This family studies the boundaries between those three categories. The central object is a synthetic offline audit environment, designed so that the model may succeed, the ordinary rival may win, or a safety policy may correctly refuse the request. Five separate flagship questions meet at the same test bench. F076 tests the intervention fidelity of explanations; F077 asks whether unfamiliar inputs can be recognized before acceptance; F078 audits the source lineage and disparate failures that can manufacture attractive evaluation scores; F079 gives authorization a separate and explicit place in the decision path; F080 measures the usefulness of quantum-labelled computation after whole-pipeline cost. Each flagship has its own failure conditions. Their coupling is useful only if interfaces are causal, auditable and independently replaceable. Interpretability is especially vulnerable to beautiful output. Heatmaps, feature masks and counterfactual diagrams can look precise while merely expressing local correlation or an approximate post hoc surrogate. A serious explanatory claim tells the next investigator which feasible feature intervention will change the prediction and which independent witness can confirm it. A neural feature that was never intervened on cannot be declared causal from the color of a plot. Distribution shifts change the meaning of confidence. The familiar recording can be transformed by a new electrode montage, a different clock, an unknown class or missing-channel patterns. A detector that recognizes only the noise signatures on which it was trained may appear successful while failing precisely where a reliable refusal is needed. This is why F077 preserves selective risk, coverage, false acceptance and the full latency of the veto, not just aggregate classification accuracy. Leakage often survives a superficial audit. A synthetic source can be transformed into many nearly identical examples. The copied signals may receive new filenames, be presented as a different session or pass through a normalization fitted on the entire dataset. A high score on this partition does not demonstrate that the proposed quantum model has learned generalizable neural dynamics. F078 requires source ancestry, label availability at inference time, group balance and versioned data contracts before model comparison. Human authorization has a different grammar from prediction. A permission token may be valid for one task and forbidden for another; a model version may change while a previously signed policy does not. An operator may revoke consent after inference begins. These are not situations to be resolved by increasing confidence thresholds. A correct engineering design makes the action envelope an intersection of scope, role, time and safety, independently auditable after both successful and refused requests. In this book the commands remain inert simulations. Quantum performance remains an open empirical question for the present application. A systematic review of quantum machine learning in digital health, DOI 10.1038/s41746-025-01597-z, did not find a consistent empirical advantage over classical methods. That does not forbid the search for new architectures. It does require clean experiments. Encoding overhead, noisy operations, repeated runs, queueing, mitigation, hardware drift and classical tuning all belong to a practical utility comparison. A result below the preregistered benefit threshold must be allowed to stop the search. The five-stage parallel spacetime method organizes scientific uncertainty into origin questions, mathematical proposals, competing explanations, bounded stress worlds and independently reconstructable evidence. This phrase describes intellectual branches, not physical travel through alternative universes. The stages are most useful when a late counterfactual changes what we thought we knew at the beginning. No stage gives special permission to call a hypothesis established. A technical notebook does not repeat an entire research monograph line by line. It attempts to show why a researcher would care about an experiment, how instruments might mislead, and what interpretation could survive a fair adversary. Repeated concepts are welcome when their role deepens; recycled paragraphs masquerading as new research are not. This notebook uses Mechanism, Measurement and Refutation not as decorative labels but as obligations that make one another more exact. The research is deliberately nonclinical. The proposal does not support diagnosis, implantation, robotic stroke rehabilitation or therapeutic claims. Clinical translation would require a separately approved, prospective, human-subject program with its own risk and endpoint design. Neither this document nor its figures can supply that evidence. summary: DjangoDefects is an inter-release defect prediction benchmark for Python, built from the full version history of the Django web framework. It covers 24 consecutive releases (1.0 to 5.2, September 2008 to April 2025). For every release it provides defect labels at four granularities, all derived from a single SZZ run: - File level: 20,442 file-release instances, 32.0% buggy - Method level: 169,744 function and method instances with their source code, 9.8% buggy - Line level: 14,917 buggy source lines - AST-node level: 5.38 M nodes from a full DFS traversal of each affected file's AST, with typed parent edges (ready to load as a graph), 1.29% buggy A source snapshot of every release is included. All file paths, method spans, line numbers and node spans refer to the code exactly as it shipped in that release. Construction. 5,585 closed, fixed Bug tickets from Django's Trac issue tracker were linked to 4,801 fix commits through Fixed #<ticket> references. Each fix was traced back to the commits that introduced the bug using SZZ Unleashed, with whitespace-insensitive blame and whitespace and comment filters, giving 6,306 bug records. Fixes that only add code, such as a missing check, change no existing line that blame could trace. Each one is attributed instead to the nearest code line above the insertion point. This adds 1,914 bug records, which label files and methods only. Releases are assigned by git ancestry rather than by date, which accounts for Django forking each stable branch months before the release tag. Buggy lines are located in each release snapshot by blame identity. Contents. - file_level.zip, method_level.zip, line_level.zip, ast_level.zip: one CSV per release - source_code.zip: every file under django/ at each release tag - code.zip: the pipeline that generated the dataset, the cached ticket-to-commit links, and instructions for reproducing it - README.md: full documentation, including schemas, statistics and threats to validity Intended uses. - Cross-version defect prediction at file and method level - Fine-grained defect localisation at line and AST-node level - Training models that use code structure, such as graph neural networks on the ASTs or code language models on method source Known limitations. - Labels for the most recent releases (about 5.0 to 5.2) are incomplete, because many of their bugs have not been reported or fixed yet. - File and method labels cover every release in which a bug is present. Line and node labels cover only the release that introduced it. - Labels from fixes that only add code are a heuristic. The anchor line can be older than the bug itself, so these bugs may start a few releases too early. They are marked label_source = added_only and can be filtered out. - See README.md §7 for the other threats to validity. Changes in 2.0.0. Fixes that only add code now label files and methods, which adds 746 buggy file-release instances and 2,474 buggy method-release instances. A new label_source column (removed / added_only) in the file- and method-level CSVs marks where each label comes from. Keeping only rows with label_source = removed reproduces the 1.0.0 labels exactly. The line, AST-node and source-code files are unchanged. Licence. The labels, documentation and code are released under CC BY 4.0. The included Django source code is © Django Software Foundation and individual contributors, redistributed under its BSD-3-Clause licence (LICENSE-DJANGO).

summary: Input data for the replication package of Heilmayr, R. and Benedict, J., “Rising risk of deforestation in Indonesia’s pulp sector”. The code is at https://github.com/jasonjb82/heilmayr-indo-pulp-deforestation-2026 . summary: MDPSolver 0.12.0 Faster, with less memory : the transition probabilities are now stored in compressed sparse rows (CSR) and read by direct loops, and each sum is split over four partial sums. Large models given as arrays solve 9–12× faster end to end than with 0.11.0, with 3.4–4.6× less peak memory. On one thread, value iteration is 2.4–3.6× faster on models with many next states per state and action. Against pymdptoolbox, MDPSolver is now up to 719× faster with policy iteration, 407× with modified policy iteration and 6.2× with value iteration (see the wiki page Performance experiments ). New: NumPy arrays as input : every input format of mdp() accepts NumPy arrays, and lists still work. As arrays, every state has the same number of actions, and tranMatProbs / tranMatColumns pad state-action pairs with fewer entries with the probability 0. As lists, or in the elementwise formats, states may still have different numbers of actions. New: float32 transition probabilities : transition probabilities given as float32 are kept as float32, which takes 8 instead of 12 bytes per non-zero probability. Rounded to float32, the probabilities of a state and action sum to 1 only to within about 1e-7. That can take the solver more iterations, and limits the tolerance it can reach under the average reward criterion. New: NPY files : rewardsFromFile and tranMatFromFile read NumPy .npy files, recognised by the .npy extension, straight into the solver, so the model is never held in Python. The files hold the elementwise rows ( [state, action, reward] and [from_state, action, to_state, probability] ) as float64, float32, int64 or int32. A model with 1 billion non-zero transition probabilities loads in 19 seconds, instead of 9 minutes from CSV files, with the same peak memory. CSV files work as before. See the wiki page Loading models from NPY files . New: Python threads : solve() lets other Python threads run while it computes, so models in several threads are solved at the same time. Calls on one model object still run one at a time. Bug fix : CSV files with more than 2^31 (about 2.1 billion) lines overflowed the loader's line counter, which made errors name wrong line numbers. Outputs : getPolicy() and getValueVector() now return NumPy arrays (int64 and float64) instead of lists. Dependency : NumPy is now required, and pip installs it with MDPSolver. Results : values can differ from those of 0.11.0 in the last digits (relative differences up to about 1e-14), since the sums are now added in a different order. Policies and iteration counts were unchanged in our tests. Tests : two new unit tests cover NumPy arrays and Python threads, and the import test now covers .npy files. Documentation : the README has a new performance table, with models up to 1 billion non-zero transition probabilities, and the benchmark against pymdptoolbox was rerun with the newest versions of both packages. Backward compatible with 0.11.0, except for the outputs: code that compares getPolicy() or getValueVector() with a list, passes them to json.dumps , or uses list methods on them needs .tolist() , e.g. mdl.getPolicy().tolist() . Verified across Linux, Windows, and macOS before release.

summary: This record is the replication package for the paper "New rules, old habits: across seven team sports, each league keeps its own way of using the rules" (Gustavo Pedro Ricou, Trinity College Dublin). It holds the paper and its supplement, the code that computes and checks every number they print, the hand-built evidence that no script can rebuild, and the result tables every number is computed from. Why the manuscript is archived here. The manuscript is archived with its code and data, not as a second place of publication, because the three are one object. Every number in the paper is computed from the archived result tables by the archived code, and the archived tests fail if the text and the tables disagree. So the version of record of the evidence includes the version of the text it supports, and a reader can check any sentence of the paper against the data behind it. The preprint is arXiv:2609.05584; this record is its data complement. Versions. Version v1.0.0 of this record held the first version of the preprint, a nine-sport paper on how playing time is allocated. Versions v2.0.0 and v2.0.1 hold its second version. Version v2.0.1 carries the same paper and the same numbers as v2.0.0. Its archive holds only the files the paper's builders and tests use. What the paper does. Studies of a rule change usually report one average effect. This paper asks whether a rule change reorders the leagues, in 101 leagues of seven sports. When football's substitution limit rose from three to five, the fourteen top leagues kept their order into the first season under five (rank correlation 0.89). That is about as firmly as from one ordinary season to the next. A prediction for twelve second tiers, written before their records were read, held (0.73), and they ranked like their own country's top league. Across rule changes in other sports, leagues kept their order in four of eight tests. In every sport measured, a league stayed near its place among its sport's leagues from season to season. So a rule change is best judged league by league, against each league's own seasons. What is in the files. source-v2.0.1.tar.gz : the manuscript and supplement sources with their generated tables, among them the audit of the pre-specification (paper_b/), and the files that the paper's builders and tests open, measured by a trace of their runs, as the tagged commit paper2-v2.0.1 holds them, unchanged. Those files are the pipeline's stages (src/), the tests (tests/), the builders (tools/), the hand-built evidence (data/manual/: the rule limits, the registers of pre-specified tests and an extract of the repository host's push log) and the plan of stages 361 to 368 (docs/). A README, the LICENSE, CITATION.cff and a checksum for every file (SHA256SUMS-source.txt) are added. derived-outputs-v2.0.1.tar.gz : the 156 result tables that the paper's builders and tests read, which are the minimum dataset needed to verify every claim, with a checksum for every table (SHA256SUMS-tables.txt). manuscript.pdf and supplement.pdf : the paper and its supplement, compiled from the tagged sources. SHA256SUMS.txt : the SHA-256 checksum of each of the four files above. The archives are built deterministically, with sorted entries, no owner and fixed timestamps. So a rebuild from the same tag gives the same bytes, and the checksums mean what they say. From the two archives alone, all of the paper's gate tests pass but one, which reads a third-party index of competitions that cannot be redistributed. Licence carve-out. Three different terms apply inside this record. The data compilation and the documentation are released under CC BY 4.0. The code is released under the MIT Licence, whose text is in LICENSE inside the source archive. The manuscript and supplement files (manuscript.pdf, supplement.pdf and the sources under paper_b/) are (c) the author and are expressly NOT released under CC BY, pending journal publication. The record's licence field reads CC BY 4.0 because Zenodo all

summary: Python code, extracted data and stored results for the paper "When can reinfection sustain tuberculosis  below R0 = 1? A general criterion and its practical identifiability from Ugandan surveillance data". The archive contains the symbolic derivations and numerical checks of the general reinfection criterion  (entry and target distributions, centre-manifold coefficients, several susceptible classes, recruitment proportional to population size) and of its special cases (Safan et al. 2006; Song 2021; Wang et al. 2023; Feng, Castillo-Chavez and Capurro 2000), the analysis of the two-stage latency model, the calibration to            Ugandan tuberculosis notifications 2000-2025 (2025 provisional), the 2014-2015 national prevalence survey and treatment-history data, the profile likelihoods (with dispersion and autocorrelation adjustments), the  uncertainty, HIV and relapse analyses, the figure scripts and the LaTeX templates from which every number in the paper is generated. See README.txt. Requires Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, pandas, Matplotlib and Numba. Versions 1.0 and 2.0 accompanied earlier versions of the paper.

The archive contains the symbolic derivations and numerical checks of the general reinfection criterion  (entry and target distributions, centre-manifold coefficients, several susceptible classes, recruitment proportional to population size) and of its special cases (Safan et al. 2006; Song 2021; Wang et al. 2023; Feng, Castillo-Chavez and Capurro 2000), the analysis of the two-stage latency model, the calibration to            Ugandan tuberculosis notifications 2000-2025 (2025 provisional), the 2014-2015 national prevalence survey and treatment-history data, the profile likelihoods (with dispersion and autocorrelation adjustments), the  uncertainty, HIV and relapse analyses, the figure scripts and the LaTeX templates from which every number in the paper is generated. See README.txt. Requires Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, pandas, Matplotlib and Numba. Versions 1.0 and 2.0 accompanied earlier versions of the paper.

summary: Speaker representation learning is fundamental to speech processing tasks such as speaker verification and diarization. Although long-context speaker encoders can produce stable and discriminative embeddings, short-duration verification and diarization require finer-grained temporal representations. Short temporal contexts limit the available speaker evidence and make speaker identity difficult to disentangle from phonetic and acoustic variability. This creates a temporal resolution-representation reliability trade-off: speaker representations should maintain local within-speaker consistency, between-speaker discriminability and remain sensitive to speaker changes at fine temporal resolution. Accordingly, we propose a framework for reliable speaker representation learning at fine temporal resolution. FineSpeaker first constructs resolution-controllable frame-wise speaker representations through mean pooling over an adjustable n-frame window, enabling flexible control of representation granularity. It then introduces a speaker encoder with local temporal modeling that exploits short-range speaker context to improve the stability and discriminability of short-duration and frame-wise representations. Furthermore, we develop a generative disentanglement strategy for optimizing frame-level speaker representations, combining VAE-based probabilistic modeling with flow matching to characterize speaker-related variation and suppress non-speaker interference. Experiments demonstrate competitive full-utterance performance, improved fine-grained speaker verification on VoxCeleb and CN-Celeb, and strong zero-shot diarization results, highlighting the benefits of balancing temporal resolution and representation reliability.
title: FineSpeaker: Reliable Speaker Representation Learning at Fine Temporal Resolution

summary: This document describes the measurement setup, signal processing, data organization, and MATLAB file format of a database of acoustic responses measured on a Knowles Electronics Manikin for Acoustic Research (KEMAR) using the Hearpiece, a multi-microphone, multi-driver in-ear research device. The data include binaural room impulse responses (BRIRs) and Hearpiece driver responses, together with center-microphone room impulse responses and a loopback impulse response of the playback and recording system. The BRIRs cover two Hearpiece configurations, three room conditions, three independent insertions per configuration, and 24 horizontal source directions. The database supports reproducible research on binaural and hearing-device signal processing, with potential applications in speech enhancement, spatial filtering and source separation, dereverberation, active noise and occlusion control, and acoustic feedback cancellation. The database, MATLAB loading script, and technical documentation are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23667308.
title: The Hearpiece Database of Binaural Room Impulse Responses and Driver Responses on KEMAR

summary: This paper studies the capability of an object-centric audio representation to support multiple downstream tasks within a unified framework. The object-centric model is trained in a self-supervised setup using slot attention by reconstructing Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) patch embeddings from a set of latent slots. It is trained on synthetic audio mixtures, which provides controlled multi-source audio scenes. These slot representations are evaluated for the classification, detection, and separation of sound events by training task specific output layers. On the classification task, the model achieves an F1-score of 0.8, comparable to clip-level AST embeddings which achieve 0.7. For sound event detection, it reaches a macro F1-score of 0.7, outperforming clip-level AST embeddings at 0.4 and matching AST patch embeddings at 0.7, which encode finer time-frequency information. In source separation, it achieves an SI-SDR improvement (SI-SDRi) of 18.4 dB. Furthermore, in a zero-shot source separation setting, the model achieves an SI-SDRi of 14.5 dB. These results demonstrate that slot-based representations capture transferable and compositional structure in audio scenes, enabling generalization across tasks and datasets.
title: Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representation for Multi-Task Audio Analysis

summary: Video-queried sound separation (VQSS) aims to isolate a target sound from an audio mixture using its corresponding video as a query. However, scene-level video queries can become ambiguous when multiple sounding objects are visible, particularly when the target and interferer are semantically similar. We propose SelectSep, a target-selective VQSS framework that jointly uses text and a single click coordinate to specify the target source and instance without requiring segmentation at inference time. We adapt the visual encoder through target-feature distillation with text and click conditioning, and then fine-tune the separator using the adapted visual features. We also introduce an on-screen interference setting, where both the target and interferer are visible, to evaluate target selectivity. Experiments on standard benchmarks and the on-screen interference setting demonstrate consistent improvements in separation quality and target selectivity, particularly for mixtures containing semantically similar sources.
title: SelectSep: Target-Selective Video Queries for Audio Source Separation

summary: Many real-world signals are corrupted by localized, structured perturbations whose distribution is unknown: an intermittent background noise in a music recording, a watermark stamped on a photograph, a cast shadow. We study the task of recovering a clean signal $x$ from an observation $y$ containing such a localized out-of-distribution (OOD) corruption. We propose Support-guided OOD Removal with Diffusion, SORD, an iterative algorithm to recover $x$ using only two ingredients: a binary map of the corruption support and a single diffusion model pretrained on clean signals. SORD does not require any paired data or any statistical model of the corruption. We evaluate SORD on natural images and human faces with spatially localized corruptions including handwritten digits, other images, watermarks, and shadows, as well as audio recordings of different musical instruments with temporally localized corruptions including other instruments and human speech. SORD is competitive with, and often outperforms, posterior-sampling inpainting given the same diffusion prior and the same mask, source-separation baselines that require a separate diffusion model for each source, and, on several benchmarks, supervised networks trained on paired clean and corrupted signals. The code is released here: \href{https://github.com/voilalab/SORD}{https://github.com/voilalab/SORD}.

summary: Generative target speaker extraction (TSE) models achieve high-quality extraction, but suffer from considerably slow training convergence. Representation Alignment (REPA) accelerates diffusion transformer training by aligning hidden states with a pre-trained Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) teacher. However, existing alignment in the speech and audio domain operates at a single granularity. For TSE, frame-level alignment leaves the global, time-invariant characteristics of the target speech implicit, whereas utterance-level alignment leaves the time-varying content implicit, even though extracting the target requires both. We propose Multi-Granularity Representation Alignment (MG-REPA), aligning the hidden states with an SSL model at the frame level and a speaker verification model at the utterance level. We further apply temporal normalization to the frame-level target, removing its utterance-level statistics so that each branch concentrates on its granularity. On Libri2Mix, MG-REPA reaches the OVRL and PESQ of a MeanFlow-TSE baseline with $3.0\times$ and $2.1\times$ fewer epochs, respectively. Trained for 750 epochs, it is competitive with the published 2,000-epoch baseline on intrusive metrics while improving non-intrusive metrics. An ablation demonstrates that MG-REPA outperforms alignment at a single granularity.
title: MG-REPA: Multi-Granularity Representation Alignment for Generative Target Speaker Extraction

summary: Large self-supervised speech models provide powerful representations for speaker verification, but full fine-tuning is expensive. Most conventional adapters insert small trainable modules to modify the output of each layer, while keeping the original residual connections unchanged. Building on our preliminary study of manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections in speaker encoders, we explore parameter-efficient adaptation of both residual paths and feature selection across layers. We first propose a Manifold-Constrained Residual Adapter (MCRA), which splits the hidden dimensions of each Transformer residual state into N groups and uses a small Sinkhorn-normalized matrix to exchange information among them. A learnable gate controls the balance between the original and mixed residual paths. The gate adds only one scalar parameter at each residual connection and initially favors the original path, allowing gradual adaptation. We further propose Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation (FALA), an attention-based aggregation method that uses a single learned query shared across all utterances to compute layer weights separately for each speech frame. Because the layer representations depend on the input, the resulting weights vary across both utterances and frames, unlike the fixed weights of a conventional layer-weighted sum. Compared with a frozen WavLM baseline using a fixed layer-weighted sum, our method achieves relative EER reductions of 22.4% on VoxCeleb1-O and 2.9% on CN-Celeb, with trainable adaptation parameters equivalent to only 0.0009% and 0.0016% of the WavLM-Large parameters, respectively.
title: Manifold-Constrained Residual Adaptation with Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation for Speaker Verification

summary: End-to-end neural diarization with vector clustering (EEND-VC) is a strong framework for long-form conversational diarization, where speaker embeddings are used to link local speaker decisions across windows. Conventional EEND-VC systems extract these embeddings by cutting out regions assigned to each local speaker, preferably using only non-overlapped speech. This works well when enough clean target-speaker speech is available, but it discards useful speaker evidence in overlapped regions and becomes unreliable when a local speaker appears mostly in overlap. We propose a speaker-activity-conditioned embedding extractor that adapts a pretrained WavLM-MHFA speaker verification model to extract target-speaker embeddings directly from full conversational windows. Inspired by the recently proposed diarization-conditioned Whisper (DiCoW) model for target-speaker ASR, frame-level diarization-dependent transformations inject local speaker-activity information into intermediate WavLM representations while preserving the pretrained initialization. Experiments on multiple conversational diarization benchmarks show that fine-tuning with limited real meeting data reduces speaker-confusion errors and improves EEND-VC diarization performance. The results further indicate that real conversational data provides an effective alternative to large-scale simulated-mixture training for diarization-aware speaker embedding extraction.

summary: Target speaker extraction (TSE) isolates a desired speaker from a multi-speaker mixture using cues that identify the target. Prior work has explored acoustic and textual cues, such as enrollment audio and different types of speaker descriptors, but typically relies on a single cue family. Yet no single cue is both broadly available and reliably discriminative. Moreover, most TSE systems adopt mask-prediction models, which are prone to audible artifacts and generalize poorly across acoustic conditions. To address these limitations, we propose PromptSep-Speaker, a generative TSE model based on latent diffusion that unifies four interchangeable cues: speaker temporal order, transcript, enrollment audio, and speaker caption. The generative formulation delivers higher separation quality and multi-modal prompting improves applicability across scenarios. To fully exploit each cue, we further introduce a frozen WavLM representation with an auxiliary alignment loss that supervises query-mixture cross-attention without extra labeling. Across four evaluation sets and a listening study, PromptSep-Speaker achieves state-of-the-art performance over TSE and universal source separation baselines, improving separation accuracy and quality across cue modalities.
title: PromptSep-Speaker: Generative Target Speaker Extraction via Multimodal Prompting and Semantic Alignment

summary: Drum beats are often conceptualized and produced as arrangements of repeated single-drum sound events or one-shots. Drum Analysis-by-Synthesis (AbS) models combine this structural assumption with reconstruction-based training to perform MIR tasks such as drum transcription, drum source separation, and one-shot extraction, offering a flexible alternative to more traditional task-specific supervision. However, leading AbS approaches struggle to generalize to a broad range of drum timbres (e.g., electronic drum kits), rely on high-quality paired audio-transcription training data, and do not model intra-class timbral variation within a single arrangement (e.g., multiple kick sounds). To overcome these limitations, we propose D-Composer, an autoregressive language modeling framework that decomposes drum recordings into labeled sound events and their onset times. In drum transcription and one-shot extraction tasks, D-Composer performs comparably to or better than a state-of-the-art AbS system and task-specific baselines while generalizing to a broader range of drum timbres. Our results demonstrate that when equipped with abundant synthetic data and compact acoustic token representations, language modeling provides a simple recipe for unifying transcription and sound event decomposition.
title: D-Composer: Language Modeling for Simultaneous Drum Transcription and Sound Event Decomposition
